text:
Production 3-tier web architecture on AWS

The baseline reference: ALB in public subnets across 3 AZs → ECS/EKS application tier in private subnets across 3 AZs → RDS Multi-AZ in isolated data subnets. WAF in front of the ALB, CloudFront for static assets and edge caching, S3 for object storage, ElastiCache for session/cache. Every tier has its own Security Group, referencing the SG of the tier above it (web-sg → app-sg → db-sg). This is the safe default for any web-style workload — if you do not have a strong reason to deviate, ship this.

Decision rules:
- DEPLOY across 3 AZs minimum for production (2 AZs is staging)
- USE ALB for HTTP(S), NLB for TCP/UDP or extreme throughput, API Gateway for serverless / fine-grained throttling
- ENABLE WAF managed rule sets (AWS Managed Rules Common, Known Bad Inputs, SQLi)
- PUT CloudFront in front of any externally-facing endpoint — DDoS protection (Shield Standard) + edge cache + lower data-transfer cost
- RDS Multi-AZ for production; consider Aurora over RDS for >100GB databases or read-replica-heavy workloads

Trade-offs:
- 3 AZs: max availability vs higher NAT gateway and data-transfer cost
- Aurora vs RDS: better performance and HA vs higher cost and AWS-only
- ALB vs API Gateway: ALB cheaper and lower-latency vs API Gateway has built-in throttling, auth, mappings

Anti-patterns:
- Single-AZ deployment for production — one AZ event takes the service down
- Public IPs on application instances 'for SSH' — use Session Manager
- RDS in a public subnet 'so the BI team can connect' — use a bastion or AWS Client VPN

metadata.title: Production 3-tier web architecture on AWS

text:
Production EKS topology for microservice workloads

EKS managed control plane in 3 AZs; managed node groups (mix of On-Demand and Spot) provisioned by Karpenter; AWS VPC CNI for pod networking; AWS Load Balancer Controller for ALB/NLB ingress; ExternalDNS for Route 53; cert-manager for TLS; Argo CD for GitOps; OpenTelemetry Collector as DaemonSet; Falco for runtime detection; OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno for policy. IRSA for workload IAM. NetworkPolicy default-deny per namespace. Secrets via External Secrets Operator from AWS Secrets Manager.

Decision rules:
- ONE production cluster per region per environment — multi-tenancy via namespaces, not multi-cluster, until ~500 services
- USE Karpenter for node provisioning, not Cluster Autoscaler — better Spot diversification and bin-packing
- GITOPS (Argo CD or Flux) is the only path to apply manifests in prod — kubectl apply by humans is forbidden
- ENFORCE PodSecurityStandard `restricted` in every workload namespace; `baseline` only for kube-system
- RUN admission policy (Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper) blocking: privileged pods, hostPath, default ServiceAccount usage, missing resource requests

Trade-offs:
- Karpenter: faster, denser packing vs newer than Cluster Autoscaler
- Argo CD vs Flux: Argo has a UI and is the de facto standard; Flux is leaner and more modular
- AWS Load Balancer Controller (ALB per Ingress) vs nginx ingress (one ALB, host-based routing): ALB-per-Ingress isolates blast radius; nginx is cheaper at scale

Anti-patterns:
- One giant cluster for prod and non-prod — blast radius is unacceptable
- Helm chart per-team without a central platform team — consistency and security policy drift
- Skipping admission policy — security guardrails as code review only is unreliable

metadata.title: Production EKS topology for microservice workloads

text:
AWS landing zone with Organizations, Control Tower, and SCPs

A multi-account strategy is the strongest blast-radius control AWS offers. Use AWS Organizations with Control Tower to bootstrap: a Management account (billing, Organizations only — never run workloads here), Log Archive (immutable CloudTrail/Config logs), Audit (read-only security tooling), and per-team / per-environment workload accounts (dev/staging/prod separated). Service Control Policies (SCPs) enforce guardrails that even account admins cannot bypass.

Decision rules:
- ONE production account per business unit / per environment — not 'one prod account for everything'
- MANAGEMENT account runs no workloads — only billing, Organizations, and Identity Center (SSO)
- LOG ARCHIVE account is the centralized destination for CloudTrail (org trail), Config, and S3 access logs — immutable bucket policy with object lock
- SCPs at the OU level enforce guardrails: deny disabling CloudTrail/Config, deny region usage outside approved list, deny IAM user creation, deny S3 public-access toggle
- USE AWS Identity Center (SSO) with permission sets mapped to SAML/OIDC IdP groups — no IAM users in workload accounts

Trade-offs:
- More accounts: stronger isolation vs more accounts to manage — Control Tower and Account Factory automate the long tail
- Strict SCPs: tight guardrails vs frustration when a legit need is blocked — use OUs to scope SCPs
- Centralized logging: clean audit vs cross-account log shipping cost

Anti-patterns:
- Running workloads in the management account — privilege concentration disaster
- One IAM user per developer per account — Identity Center exists for a reason
- SCPs that allow * — provides no guardrail

metadata.title: AWS landing zone with Organizations, Control Tower, and SCPs

text:
RTO/RPO patterns: Backup, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Region Active-Active

DR strategy is a function of acceptable downtime (RTO) and acceptable data loss (RPO). The four canonical AWS DR strategies trade cost for recovery speed: Backup & Restore (RTO hours, cheapest), Pilot Light (RTO ~1h, core infra running, app dormant), Warm Standby (RTO minutes, scaled-down replica running), Multi-Region Active-Active (RTO seconds, expensive). Most workloads do not need active-active; matching DR to actual business RTO/RPO saves significant cost.

Decision rules:
- DEFINE RTO/RPO from the business owner — not from the engineering wishlist
- BACKUP & RESTORE for non-critical workloads (RTO 4-24h, RPO hours): AWS Backup, cross-region copy
- PILOT LIGHT for critical-but-not-tier-0 (RTO 1-4h, RPO minutes): keep VPC, RDS read-replica, IAM in DR region; spin up app on failover
- WARM STANDBY for tier-1 (RTO 5-30m, RPO seconds): scaled-down full stack in DR region, scale up on failover
- ACTIVE-ACTIVE for tier-0 (RTO seconds, RPO sub-second): Aurora Global / DynamoDB Global Tables, Route 53 latency routing
- TEST DR quarterly with real failover — untested DR is not DR

Trade-offs:
- Active-active: lowest RTO vs highest cost (~2x) and data-consistency complexity (conflict resolution)
- Pilot Light: cheap insurance vs requires automation that has been rehearsed
- Cross-region backup: cheap vs RTO measured in hours — only acceptable for non-critical data

Anti-patterns:
- Single-region 'Multi-AZ is enough' for tier-0 — regional outages happen (us-east-1 has had several)
- DR plan that has never been tested — first failover during a real incident is the worst time to find bugs
- Active-active without conflict-resolution strategy — silent data corruption

metadata.title: RTO/RPO patterns: Backup, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Region Active-Active

text:
Hybrid connectivity: Direct Connect, VPN, and Outposts

Hybrid is common for regulated industries, large existing on-prem footprints, or data-sovereignty constraints. AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the public internet is fast to set up but limited to ~1.25 Gbps per tunnel and depends on internet. Direct Connect provides dedicated 1/10/100 Gbps with predictable latency but takes weeks to provision and requires colo presence. Use Direct Connect + VPN as backup. AWS Outposts extends the AWS control plane into your data center for true hybrid workloads.

Decision rules:
- USE Site-to-Site VPN for ≤1 Gbps, dev/staging hybrid, or as Direct Connect backup
- USE Direct Connect for production hybrid: ≥1 Gbps sustained, latency-sensitive, or compliance prohibits internet path
- ALWAYS pair Direct Connect with VPN backup — DX outages do happen
- ATTACH DX/VPN to Transit Gateway, not directly to a VPN gateway — TGW scales to many VPCs
- USE Outposts when latency-critical workloads must be on-prem AND you want the AWS control plane (rare; expensive)

Trade-offs:
- Direct Connect: predictable performance vs weeks to provision, monthly port fee
- Multiple DX connections (different locations): true HA vs more cost
- Outposts: AWS-native hybrid vs expensive, capacity-locked

Anti-patterns:
- Single Direct Connect with no VPN backup — single fiber cut takes the link down
- Hybrid via internet VPN for production payment workloads — latency and reliability are not enough
- VPN to a single VPN Gateway when scaling beyond 2-3 VPCs — TGW is the right primitive

metadata.title: Hybrid connectivity: Direct Connect, VPN, and Outposts

text:
VPC Architecture — Multi-AZ Public/Private Subnet Design

A production VPC uses a multi-AZ layout with strict tier separation: public subnets (internet-facing load balancers, NAT gateways), private application subnets (compute: ECS, EKS nodes, EC2), and private data subnets (RDS, ElastiCache, Elasticsearch). This is the AWS-recommended baseline for any production workload. The VPC CIDR must be planned for future growth and VPC peering requirements.

Decision rules:
- USE /16 CIDR for production VPCs — allows 65,536 IPs and room for subnet division across 3+ AZs
- USE /24 subnets per tier per AZ as default — 251 usable IPs per subnet is sufficient for most service tiers
- DEPLOY across minimum 2 AZs for staging, 3 AZs for production — ensures regional failover tolerance
- PLACE load balancers (ALB/NLB) in public subnets only — compute resources must NEVER be directly internet-exposed
- PLACE compute (EKS nodes, ECS tasks, EC2) in private application subnets — no public IPs
- PLACE databases (RDS, ElastiCache) in isolated private data subnets — no route to application subnets except via security groups
- AVOID CIDR overlap with on-premises networks or other VPCs if VPC peering or Transit Gateway is planned

Trade-offs:
- 3-AZ deployment: high availability vs. 50% higher NAT gateway cost and subnet count
- Separate data subnets: strong isolation vs. requires more subnet management and route tables
- Large VPC CIDR: future flexibility vs. CIDR exhaustion in multi-VPC architectures
- Single VPC vs. multi-VPC: simpler networking vs. blast radius contains entire application

Anti-patterns:
- Placing RDS or ElastiCache in public subnets — violates security baseline, exposes data plane to internet
- Using overlapping CIDRs across VPCs in the same account — blocks future peering and Transit Gateway
- Deploying all resources in a single AZ — single AZ failure causes complete outage
- Assigning public IPs to EC2 instances in application subnets — bypasses NAT and exposes private services
- Creating a flat VPC with no subnet tier separation — prevents security group isolation and blast radius control

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: tier separation limits lateral movement in the event of a breach
- Reliability Pillar: multi-AZ deployment tolerates AZ-level failures
- Cost Optimization: right-sized subnets prevent IP exhaustion while avoiding unnecessary scale

metadata.title: VPC Architecture — Multi-AZ Public/Private Subnet Design

text:
NAT Gateway vs. NAT Instance

NAT Gateways provide managed outbound internet connectivity for private subnet resources. They are fully managed by AWS, scale automatically, and require no patching. NAT Instances are self-managed EC2 instances functioning as NAT — they are a legacy pattern with significant operational overhead. In any production environment, NAT Gateway is the unambiguous choice.

Decision rules:
- USE NAT Gateway for all production workloads — no exceptions
- DEPLOY one NAT Gateway per AZ for production — cross-AZ NAT traffic incurs data transfer fees and AZ dependency
- USE a single NAT Gateway for dev/staging environments to optimize cost — accept the single-AZ risk
- CONSIDER VPC Endpoints (Gateway and Interface) to eliminate NAT costs for AWS service traffic (S3, DynamoDB, ECR, SSM)
- USE NAT Instance ONLY for cost-constrained personal projects — not in any business workload

Trade-offs:
- Per-AZ NAT Gateway: zero cross-AZ data charges, full HA vs. 3x NAT Gateway cost (~$32/mo each)
- Single NAT Gateway: 66% cost reduction vs. AZ-level failure disrupts all private subnet outbound traffic
- VPC Endpoints: eliminates NAT data charges for AWS services vs. per-endpoint hourly cost (~$7/mo each)

Anti-patterns:
- Using NAT Instance in production — patching burden, no auto-scaling, becomes a bottleneck
- Single NAT Gateway in production with SLA requirements — AZ failure = all private resources lose internet
- Not using S3 Gateway Endpoint — S3 traffic through NAT incurs unnecessary data transfer cost (S3 Gateway Endpoint is free)

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: per-AZ NAT eliminates AZ-level single points of failure
- Cost Optimization: VPC Endpoints reduce NAT data processing charges for high-volume AWS service calls

metadata.title: NAT Gateway vs. NAT Instance

text:
VPC Endpoints — Reducing Attack Surface and Egress Cost

VPC Endpoints allow private connectivity to AWS services without routing through the public internet or NAT Gateway. Gateway Endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free and routing-based. Interface Endpoints (most other services: ECR, SSM, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch, STS) use ENIs in your subnet and have hourly costs. For security-sensitive workloads, Interface Endpoints prevent all AWS API traffic from leaving the VPC.

Decision rules:
- ALWAYS create S3 Gateway Endpoint and DynamoDB Gateway Endpoint in every VPC — they are free and reduce NAT cost
- CREATE Interface Endpoints for ECR (required for EKS nodes in private subnets to pull images)
- CREATE Interface Endpoints for SSM, SSMMessages, EC2Messages when using AWS Systems Manager Session Manager
- CREATE Interface Endpoints for Secrets Manager, KMS when secrets access must not traverse the internet
- EVALUATE Interface Endpoint cost vs. NAT savings for high-volume services — break-even at moderate API call volume

Trade-offs:
- Full Interface Endpoint coverage: zero internet exposure for AWS APIs vs. significant endpoint hourly cost in multi-AZ
- Gateway Endpoints: free, no latency penalty vs. only covers S3 and DynamoDB
- No endpoints: simpler setup vs. AWS service traffic goes through NAT (cost + internet exposure)

Anti-patterns:
- Not creating S3 Gateway Endpoint — leaving free cost savings unclaimed while routing S3 traffic through NAT
- EKS nodes in private subnets without ECR endpoints — image pulls fail or go through NAT at high cost
- Ignoring VPC Endpoints for compliance workloads where AWS API traffic must not traverse public internet

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: keeps AWS API traffic within the AWS network, removes internet exposure
- Cost Optimization: Gateway Endpoints eliminate NAT data processing charges for S3/DynamoDB

metadata.title: VPC Endpoints — Reducing Attack Surface and Egress Cost

text:
EC2 vs. ECS Fargate vs. EKS vs. Lambda — Compute Selection Framework

Choosing the right compute primitive is the most impactful infrastructure decision. The choice determines operational complexity, scaling behavior, cost model, and deployment velocity. AWS offers a spectrum from maximum control (EC2) to zero infrastructure management (Lambda). The correct choice depends on: workload type (stateful/stateless), team Kubernetes maturity, request pattern (constant/spiky), and operational overhead tolerance.

Decision rules:
- USE Lambda WHEN: event-driven, stateless, short-lived functions (<15 min), unpredictable or spiky traffic, minimal baseline cost required
- USE ECS Fargate WHEN: containerized workload, team lacks Kubernetes expertise, need managed container orchestration without node management, microservices with moderate scale
- USE EKS WHEN: large-scale microservices, multi-team platform, Kubernetes ecosystem required (service mesh, custom operators, advanced autoscaling), stateful workloads needing persistent volumes
- USE EC2 WHEN: workload requires specific hardware (GPU, FPGA, bare metal), licensing requires dedicated hardware, applications cannot be containerized, maximum OS-level control needed
- PREFER ECS Fargate over EC2-backed ECS for new projects — removes node patching and capacity management burden
- PREFER EKS Managed Node Groups over self-managed EC2 nodes when EKS is required — AWS handles node lifecycle

Trade-offs:
- Lambda: zero idle cost, infinite scale vs. cold starts, 15-min limit, stateless-only, limited compute
- ECS Fargate: no node management vs. higher per-vCPU/GB cost than EC2, less control
- EKS: full Kubernetes power vs. highest operational complexity, ~$0.10/hr control plane cost, steep learning curve
- EC2: complete control, lowest unit cost at scale vs. patching, capacity planning, and AMI management burden

Anti-patterns:
- Using EKS for a 2-service startup — Kubernetes overhead crushes small teams (use ECS Fargate instead)
- Running long-running batch jobs on Lambda — 15-minute timeout kills incomplete jobs (use ECS or AWS Batch)
- Using EC2 for stateless web APIs that could run on Fargate — unnecessary operational overhead
- Running databases on EKS without persistent volume backup strategy — data loss risk
- Choosing Lambda for consistent high-throughput workloads — always-on Lambda is more expensive than Fargate

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Performance Efficiency: right-sizing compute to workload pattern prevents over/under-provisioning
- Cost Optimization: Fargate eliminates idle EC2 capacity; Lambda eliminates baseline cost for spiky loads
- Operational Excellence: managed services (Fargate, Lambda) reduce undifferentiated heavy lifting

metadata.title: EC2 vs. ECS Fargate vs. EKS vs. Lambda — Compute Selection Framework

text:
EKS Architecture — Node Group Strategy

When EKS is the chosen compute platform, the node group strategy determines cost, availability, and operational overhead. The standard pattern separates system workloads (kube-system) from application workloads, with a combination of On-Demand nodes for critical services and Spot instances for stateless, fault-tolerant workloads. Karpenter is the modern replacement for Cluster Autoscaler.

Decision rules:
- USE Managed Node Groups over self-managed EC2 — AWS handles node launch template, AMI, and graceful drain during upgrades
- CREATE dedicated system node group for kube-system components — prevents application workloads from starving system pods
- USE On-Demand instances for: databases, caches, stateful services, and critical path services with strict SLAs
- USE Spot instances for: batch processing, stateless APIs with horizontal scaling, CI/CD runners, development workloads
- DEPLOY Karpenter over Cluster Autoscaler for new EKS clusters — faster scale-out, bin-packing optimization, instance diversity
- USE multiple instance types in node groups — prevents single instance-type capacity exhaustion affecting scale-out
- ENABLE EKS Managed Add-ons for: VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI driver — AWS manages version upgrades

Trade-offs:
- Spot instances: 60-90% cost reduction vs. 2-minute interruption notice — only suitable for fault-tolerant workloads
- Karpenter vs. Cluster Autoscaler: faster and smarter scaling vs. newer, requires additional IRSA setup
- Managed Node Groups: easier management vs. less control over node bootstrapping and lifecycle hooks
- Large instance types: fewer nodes to manage vs. lower fault isolation granularity on node failure

Anti-patterns:
- Running stateful services (databases, Kafka) on Spot nodes — interruption causes data loss or corruption
- Single instance type in node groups — capacity shortage for that type blocks all scaling
- Not configuring Pod Disruption Budgets — node rolling updates kill too many pods simultaneously
- Mixing system and application workloads on the same nodes without taints — noisy-neighbor resource exhaustion
- Not enabling IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) — forces broad IAM permissions via node instance profile

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: Spot instances for tolerant workloads delivers 60-90% compute savings
- Reliability: On-Demand for critical paths, Spot for batch — right reliability level per workload
- Security Pillar: IRSA provides pod-level IAM isolation instead of broad node-level permissions

metadata.title: EKS Architecture — Node Group Strategy

text:
S3 vs. EBS vs. EFS vs. RDS — Storage Selection Framework

AWS storage primitives serve fundamentally different access patterns. S3 is object storage for unstructured data with essentially infinite scale. EBS is block storage attached to a single EC2 instance. EFS is shared POSIX-compliant file storage for multi-instance access. RDS provides managed relational database storage. Choosing the wrong primitive causes either data loss, performance degradation, or unnecessary cost.

Decision rules:
- USE S3 WHEN: storing objects (images, videos, backups, logs, artifacts), data lake, static website assets, ML training data
- USE EBS WHEN: EC2 instance root volumes, database storage on self-managed DB instances, applications needing block-level access
- USE EFS WHEN: multiple EC2 instances or ECS/EKS pods need concurrent read/write to the same file system (shared config, content management, ML checkpoints)
- USE RDS WHEN: relational data model, ACID transactions, structured queries, managed patching and backups are required
- USE RDS Aurora WHEN: variable load requires storage auto-scaling, multi-AZ with fast failover, or MySQL/PostgreSQL compatibility with improved performance
- USE DynamoDB WHEN: key-value or document data, massive scale, single-digit millisecond latency, serverless or Lambda-backed applications
- NEVER use EBS for shared storage between multiple instances — EBS is single-instance block storage

Trade-offs:
- S3 vs. EFS: S3 has eventual consistency (now strongly consistent), lower cost vs. EFS has POSIX semantics and low-latency file access
- RDS Multi-AZ: automatic failover, 2-3 minutes vs. ~2x cost over single-AZ
- Aurora vs. RDS: better auto-scaling, faster failover vs. Aurora Serverless v1 has cold start issues for infrequent workloads
- EFS vs. EBS for containers: shared access vs. EFS higher latency and cost for single-pod use cases

Anti-patterns:
- Using RDS for key-value lookups at scale — DynamoDB delivers better performance at lower cost
- Storing application logs in RDS — use S3 + Athena or OpenSearch instead
- Using EFS for every container storage need — EFS is expensive for single-pod access patterns (use EBS via CSI driver)
- Single-AZ RDS in production — AZ failure = database unavailable = full application outage
- Not enabling RDS automated backups — no recovery path for data corruption or accidental deletion

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: Multi-AZ RDS, S3 versioning, and EBS snapshots provide data durability
- Performance Efficiency: matching storage type to access pattern prevents bottlenecks
- Cost Optimization: S3 Intelligent-Tiering, RDS Reserved Instances reduce storage costs significantly

metadata.title: S3 vs. EBS vs. EFS vs. RDS — Storage Selection Framework

text:
ALB vs. NLB — Load Balancer Selection

AWS offers two primary load balancer types for production workloads. Application Load Balancer (ALB) operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) with content-based routing, host/path rules, and native integration with WAF and Cognito. Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) with ultra-low latency, static IP addresses, and TLS passthrough. The choice is driven by protocol requirements and routing complexity.

Decision rules:
- USE ALB WHEN: HTTP/HTTPS workloads, path-based or host-based routing needed (microservices, multi-tenant SaaS), WebSocket support, WAF integration required, gRPC over HTTP/2
- USE NLB WHEN: TCP/UDP protocols (non-HTTP), ultra-low latency required (<1ms), static IP or Elastic IP needed for whitelisting, high-throughput TCP (millions of requests/sec), TLS passthrough to backend
- USE ALB with ECS and EKS for most web applications — native target group integration and health check flexibility
- USE NLB in front of ALB ONLY when static IPs are required for ALB (NLB preserves source IP, ALB does not natively)
- ENABLE ALB access logs to S3 for compliance and security analysis
- CONFIGURE deletion protection on production load balancers — terraform apply cannot accidentally delete the LB

Trade-offs:
- ALB: rich L7 routing, WAF support vs. slightly higher latency than NLB, no static IPs natively
- NLB: extreme throughput and lowest latency vs. no content-based routing, no WAF integration
- ALB idle timeout: tunable connection keep-alive vs. must match backend timeout to avoid 504s
- NLB TLS passthrough: end-to-end encryption vs. no SSL offload, certificates must be on every backend

Anti-patterns:
- Using NLB for HTTP microservices that need path-based routing — NLB cannot inspect HTTP headers
- Using ALB for non-HTTP protocols (raw TCP databases) — ALB does not support TCP pass-through
- Exposing ALB without WAF in public-facing production environments — leaves application layer unprotected
- Not setting idle timeout to match backend service timeout — causes spurious 504 errors under load
- Using Classic Load Balancer (ELB) in new deployments — legacy, missing modern features, AWS discourages new use

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: ALB + WAF protects against OWASP Top 10 at the edge
- Performance Efficiency: NLB for latency-sensitive TCP workloads avoids L7 processing overhead
- Reliability Pillar: multi-AZ LB deployment absorbs AZ-level failures transparently

metadata.title: ALB vs. NLB — Load Balancer Selection

text:
IAM Design Principles — Least Privilege and Role Architecture

IAM is the security control plane of AWS. Correct IAM design is the single most impactful security decision in any AWS architecture. The core principle is least privilege: every principal (human, service, instance, function) has the minimum permissions required to perform its function. IAM roles (not users) should be used for all machine identities. Permissions must be scoped to specific resources, not wildcards.

Decision rules:
- USE IAM Roles for all machine identities — EC2 instance profiles, ECS task roles, Lambda execution roles, EKS IRSA
- NEVER use IAM Users for programmatic access in production — use roles with AssumeRole
- SCOPE all IAM policies to specific resource ARNs — never use Resource: '*' in production policies
- SEPARATE IAM roles by function: one role per service, not a shared role for all services
- USE Service Control Policies (SCPs) at the AWS Organizations level to enforce guardrails across all accounts
- USE IAM Permission Boundaries when granting teams the ability to create roles — prevents privilege escalation
- ENABLE IAM Access Analyzer to detect overly permissive policies and external access
- USE AWS-managed policies as a baseline, then restrict — do not start from scratch for standard patterns
- APPLY IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) for Kubernetes pods — pod-level IAM instead of node-level

Trade-offs:
- Least privilege: strong security vs. operational friction when missing permissions cause application errors
- Role-per-service: precise isolation vs. IAM role limit per account (5000 default, can be increased)
- Condition-based policies (MFA, VPC source): layered security vs. complex policy authoring and debugging
- AWS-managed policies: easy to apply vs. may include more permissions than needed

Anti-patterns:
- Attaching AdministratorAccess to application roles — any credential compromise = full account compromise
- Sharing IAM roles across services — a breach of one service compromises all services sharing that role
- Using IAM Users with long-lived access keys for CI/CD — key rotation is rarely enforced, leaks are permanent until rotated
- Resource: '*' in production policies — violates least privilege, allows lateral movement
- Not using permission boundaries when allowing teams to create IAM roles — allows self-escalation to admin
- Inline policies on resources instead of managed policies — cannot be reused, audited, or version-tracked

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: IAM least privilege is the primary defense against lateral movement and privilege escalation
- Reliability: scoped permissions prevent accidental destructive API calls by services
- Operational Excellence: role-per-service enables precise security auditing and incident response

metadata.title: IAM Design Principles — Least Privilege and Role Architecture

text:
Security Groups — Network-Level Access Control

Security Groups are stateful virtual firewalls at the ENI level. They are the primary network-level access control mechanism in AWS. Unlike NACLs (stateless, subnet-level), Security Groups are stateful and attached to resources. The correct design uses Security Group chaining: SG references allow services to reference each other by security group ID rather than CIDR, providing precise service-to-service access control.

Decision rules:
- USE Security Group references (not CIDRs) for service-to-service rules — sg-xxxxxxxx as source is self-documenting and precise
- NEVER allow 0.0.0.0/0 on inbound rules except: port 443 and 80 on public ALB security groups
- CREATE one security group per service/tier — SG per RDS, per EKS node group, per ALB
- SEPARATE security groups by environment — dev and prod must never share SGs
- RESTRICT outbound rules on sensitive resources (RDS, ElastiCache) to only allow inbound from application SGs
- USE VPC Flow Logs to audit actual traffic and validate that security group rules match intent

Trade-offs:
- SG chaining: precise and readable vs. requires discipline when services are added — easy to forget to add SG rules
- CIDR-based rules: simple for external access vs. brittle when IPs change, overly broad for internal traffic
- Permissive outbound rules: zero friction for developers vs. outbound restrictions required for compliance (PCI, HIPAA)

Anti-patterns:
- Allowing 0.0.0.0/0 inbound on RDS or application security groups — direct internet exposure of data tier
- A single 'default' security group for all resources — no isolation between tiers
- Opening port ranges instead of specific ports — unnecessary attack surface
- Not regularly auditing unused security group rules — stale rules accumulate and create unintended access paths

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: micro-segmentation via SG chaining contains blast radius of compromised services
- Reliability: least-privilege network rules prevent unintended cross-tier communication failures

metadata.title: Security Groups — Network-Level Access Control

text:
Auto Scaling Design — Target Tracking vs. Step Scaling

Auto Scaling enables infrastructure to match demand dynamically. Target Tracking is the modern, preferred approach — it continuously adjusts capacity to maintain a target metric (CPU, request count, custom CloudWatch metric). Step Scaling requires manual threshold definitions and is more brittle. Scheduled scaling handles predictable load patterns. The combination of Target Tracking + scheduled scale-out before known traffic spikes is the production best practice.

Decision rules:
- USE Target Tracking scaling as default for all Auto Scaling groups and ECS services
- SET CPU target at 60-70% for web services — leaves headroom for traffic spikes during scale-out delay
- USE ALBRequestCountPerTarget metric for HTTP services — more responsive than CPU for stateless web workloads
- COMBINE Target Tracking with Scheduled Scaling for predictable spikes (e.g., scale up before market open, batch processing windows)
- SET scale-in cooldown higher than scale-out (scale-out: 60s, scale-in: 300s) — prevents thrashing
- CONFIGURE minimum instances = number of AZs to maintain multi-AZ availability at minimum capacity
- USE Predictive Scaling for recurring daily/weekly traffic patterns — pre-scales before demand arrives

Trade-offs:
- Target Tracking: simple, self-managing vs. black box — limited control over scaling behavior
- Step Scaling: precise control over scale increments vs. threshold tuning requires ongoing operational effort
- Low CPU target (50%): faster response to spikes vs. higher baseline cost from over-provisioning
- Aggressive scale-in: lower cost vs. thrashing risk when load oscillates around threshold

Anti-patterns:
- Fixed capacity (no auto scaling) for variable web workloads — either over-provisioned (wasted cost) or under-provisioned (poor UX)
- Scaling on average CPU > 90% — by the time scaling triggers, service is already degraded
- No warm-up period for scale-out — new instances serving traffic before application is ready causes 5xx errors
- Using the same scaling policy for stateful services (databases) as stateless services — state makes horizontal scaling dangerous without design changes

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: target tracking reduces idle capacity by matching supply to actual demand
- Performance Efficiency: proactive scaling prevents performance degradation under load
- Reliability: minimum capacity across AZs prevents single-AZ service disruption

metadata.title: Auto Scaling Design — Target Tracking vs. Step Scaling

text:
IAM least privilege and access analysis

IAM policies should grant only the minimum actions required. Example: allow s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on specific bucket ARN only. Use IAM Access Analyzer to find unused permissions: aws accessanalyzer create-analyzer --type ACCOUNT. Generate policies from CloudTrail activity: aws iam generate-service-last-accessed-details.

Decision rules:
- Start with deny-all and add only required actions on specific resources (not Action: '*')
- Run IAM Access Analyzer to detect overly broad permissions quarterly
- Use IAM Access Advisor to remove permissions unused for 90+ days

Trade-offs:
- Fine-grained IAM policies require more maintenance as application requirements change

Anti-patterns:
- Action: '*' or Resource: '*' in production IAM policies
- Using the AWS managed AdministratorAccess policy for application roles
- Long-lived IAM access keys — use IAM roles and temporary credentials

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Enable IAM Access Analyzer for every AWS account
- Use AWS Organizations SCPs to prevent privilege escalation across accounts

metadata.title: IAM least privilege and access analysis

text:
Encryption at rest and in transit with KMS

Create dedicated KMS keys per environment with enable_key_rotation=true and deletion_window_in_days=30. Apply SSE-KMS to S3 buckets with bucket_key_enabled=true for cost optimization. Enforce TLS 1.2+ for all data in transit.

Decision rules:
- Create one KMS key per environment (dev/staging/prod) — do not share keys across environments
- Enable automatic key rotation (enable_key_rotation=true) on all KMS keys
- Enable bucket_key_enabled=true on S3 SSE-KMS to reduce KMS API call costs

Trade-offs:
- SSE-KMS adds latency compared to SSE-S3 — acceptable for sensitive data, consider SSE-S3 for high-throughput non-sensitive data

Anti-patterns:
- Using the AWS-managed key (aws/s3) instead of a customer-managed KMS key — no key rotation control
- Transmitting data over HTTP in production — enforce TLS via bucket policies and ALB listeners

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use aws_kms_key with deletion_window_in_days >= 7 and enable_key_rotation = true
- Apply aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration with sse_algorithm = aws:kms

metadata.title: Encryption at rest and in transit with KMS

text:
VPC multi-layer architecture

Three-tier VPC: public subnets (ALB only, map_public_ip_on_launch=false), private app subnets (ECS/EKS), private data subnets (RDS). Use at least 2 AZs. Route private subnets through NAT Gateway. Use VPC Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB to avoid NAT Gateway costs.

Decision rules:
- Place ALB in public subnets, application workloads in private app subnets, databases in private data subnets
- Never assign public IPs to EC2, ECS tasks, or RDS instances directly
- Use VPC Endpoints (Gateway type for S3/DynamoDB, Interface for other services) to keep traffic on the AWS network

Trade-offs:
- NAT Gateway costs ~$35/month per AZ — use VPC Endpoints to reduce egress costs for high-volume AWS API traffic

Anti-patterns:
- Placing RDS or ElastiCache in public subnets
- Using a single NAT Gateway for multi-AZ deployments — creates an availability bottleneck

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use aws_vpc_endpoint for S3 and DynamoDB (Gateway type — free)
- Deploy NAT Gateways in each AZ for high-availability outbound internet access from private subnets

metadata.title: VPC multi-layer architecture

text:
CloudTrail for complete audit logging

Configure CloudTrail with is_multi_region_trail=true, include_global_service_events=true, enable_log_file_validation=true, KMS encryption, and S3 data event logging. Delivers comprehensive audit trail of all API activity across all regions.

Decision rules:
- Enable a multi-region trail — a single-region trail misses global service events (IAM, STS)
- Enable log file validation to detect tampering of delivered log files
- Encrypt CloudTrail logs with a dedicated KMS key (separate from application keys)

Trade-offs:
- CloudTrail logs for S3 data events generate high volume — filter to specific buckets to control costs

Anti-patterns:
- Disabling CloudTrail or limiting it to a single region
- Storing CloudTrail logs in the same account and bucket without separate S3 access controls — logs could be tampered by a compromised account

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use a dedicated Log Archive account in AWS Organizations for CloudTrail logs
- Enable AWS Config to detect CloudTrail being disabled (cloud-trail-enabled rule)

metadata.title: CloudTrail for complete audit logging

text:
GuardDuty for automated threat detection

Enable GuardDuty with S3 log analysis, Kubernetes audit log analysis, and EBS malware protection. GuardDuty uses ML and threat intelligence to detect anomalous API calls, crypto mining, compromised credentials, and lateral movement.

Decision rules:
- Enable GuardDuty in every AWS account and every region
- Enable all three data sources: s3_logs, kubernetes audit_logs, malware_protection for EBS
- Set up SNS notifications or EventBridge rules to alert on HIGH/CRITICAL findings

Trade-offs:
- GuardDuty pricing is based on data volume analyzed — S3 data events can be costly for high-traffic buckets

Anti-patterns:
- Not enabling GuardDuty — leaves the account without automated threat detection
- Enabling GuardDuty without acting on findings — security theater

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use AWS Security Hub to aggregate GuardDuty findings with other security services
- Enable GuardDuty at the AWS Organizations level via delegated administrator

metadata.title: GuardDuty for automated threat detection

text:
WAF for public API protection

Attach AWS WAFv2 WebACL to ALB or API Gateway. Configure rate limiting rule (2000 requests per 5 minutes per IP) and AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet (OWASP Top 10 protections). Enable CloudWatch metrics and sampled request logging for visibility.

Decision rules:
- Attach WAF to every public-facing ALB or API Gateway endpoint
- Start with AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and add custom rules for application-specific needs
- Set rate_based_statement limit at 2000/5-min as a starting baseline — tune based on traffic patterns

Trade-offs:
- WAF managed rules may produce false positives for legitimate traffic — use Count mode before switching to Block
- WAF adds latency (~1ms) — negligible for most workloads

Anti-patterns:
- Exposing ALBs or API Gateways to the internet without WAF
- Using WAF in Count mode permanently — rules do not block malicious traffic

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use AWS Shield Standard (included) for DDoS protection at L3/L4
- Add AWS Shield Advanced for volumetric DDoS protection on critical endpoints

metadata.title: WAF for public API protection

text:
AWS Security Baseline Checklist

Minimum security baseline for all AWS accounts: MFA on all IAM users (especially root), no root access keys, automatic KMS key rotation, S3 bucket versioning and public access block, CloudTrail enabled all regions, GuardDuty enabled, Security Hub with CIS standards, Config Rules configured, VPC Flow Logs enabled, TLS 1.2+ enforced, secrets in Secrets Manager (not env vars).

Decision rules:
- Enforce this checklist for every new AWS account before deploying any workloads
- Use AWS Security Hub CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark to track compliance automatically

Anti-patterns:
- Storing secrets in EC2 userdata, Lambda environment variables, or SSM Parameter Store Standard (not encrypted by default)
- Not enabling MFA on AWS root account — single point of compromise for entire account

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use AWS Organizations SCPs to enforce this baseline across all member accounts
- Use AWS Config conformance packs (Operational Best Practices for CIS) for automated compliance

metadata.title: AWS Security Baseline Checklist

text:
Right-sizing EC2, ECS, and EKS workloads

Most cloud overspend lives in over-provisioned compute. AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes 14 days of CloudWatch metrics and recommends instance family/size changes; for EKS, the equivalent is Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) in recommendation mode plus Goldilocks. Right-sizing should be a continuous process tied to the deploy pipeline, not a quarterly cleanup.

Decision rules:
- ENABLE Compute Optimizer org-wide; review recommendations monthly with the FinOps owner
- TARGET 60-70% average CPU and memory utilization for steady-state workloads — below 40% means oversized
- USE VPA in recommendation mode in EKS to size pod requests; do not run VPA in auto mode with HPA on the same metric
- CHOOSE Graviton (ARM) instance families for any workload that builds for ARM — typically 20-40% cheaper at equal or better performance
- PIN container CPU/memory requests to actual P95 + headroom — overprovisioned requests waste cluster capacity even with HPA

Trade-offs:
- Aggressive right-sizing: lower cost vs less burst headroom — pair with autoscaling
- Graviton: cheap and fast but requires multi-arch container images (buildx) and dependency support
- Tight pod requests: better bin-packing vs more frequent OOMKills if P95 was misestimated

Anti-patterns:
- Sizing for peak load 24/7 instead of using autoscaling
- Copy-pasting `m5.2xlarge` everywhere because it 'feels right'
- Setting Kubernetes requests = limits at high values to 'guarantee' performance — wastes cluster capacity
- Ignoring Compute Optimizer recommendations because the savings 'look small' — they compound across hundreds of instances

metadata.title: Right-sizing EC2, ECS, and EKS workloads

text:
Spot instances and mixed-instance autoscaling for stateless workloads

Spot instances run on AWS spare capacity at 60-90% discount with a 2-minute interruption notice. They are the right primitive for stateless, fault-tolerant, horizontally scalable workloads (web servers, batch jobs, CI runners, EKS worker nodes). Modern tooling (Karpenter, EKS managed node groups with Spot, EC2 Auto Scaling mixed-instances policy) makes Spot adoption nearly turnkey.

Decision rules:
- USE Spot for all stateless workloads with replicas ≥ 2 — web tier, async workers, batch, CI/CD
- DIVERSIFY across instance families and AZs (Karpenter does this automatically) — reduces correlated interruption risk
- USE On-Demand for: stateful pods (databases, leader pods), pods with long startup time (>10 min), and a small baseline (10-30%) for stability
- HANDLE the 2-minute interrupt with PodDisruptionBudgets, graceful shutdown, and AWS Node Termination Handler
- PREFER Karpenter over Cluster Autoscaler in EKS — bin-packs better, supports Spot natively, faster scale-up

Trade-offs:
- Spot: 60-90% savings vs interruption risk — diversification mitigates but does not eliminate
- Karpenter: best-in-class but relatively young — operationally simpler than Cluster Autoscaler at scale
- 100% Spot: maximum savings vs higher operational risk — keep ~10-20% On-Demand baseline

Anti-patterns:
- Running stateful pods (Postgres, Kafka, Redis) on Spot without explicit handling
- Concentrating all Spot capacity on one instance type — single price spike kills the whole fleet
- Skipping graceful shutdown handlers — connections drop mid-request on interrupt
- Using Spot for pods with 5+ minute warmup (JVM apps without CRaC, ML model loading) — interrupts faster than they start

metadata.title: Spot instances and mixed-instance autoscaling for stateless workloads

text:
Savings Plans vs Reserved Instances vs On-Demand mix

Savings Plans (Compute, EC2 Instance, SageMaker) provide 40-72% discount in exchange for a 1- or 3-year hourly $ commitment. They are more flexible than RIs (apply across regions, instance families, and Lambda/Fargate). For most workloads, the right strategy is: cover steady-state baseline with Compute Savings Plans, run elastic capacity on Spot/On-Demand, and avoid 3-year commitments unless headcount and architecture are very stable.

Decision rules:
- COMMIT (Compute Savings Plan, 1-year, no upfront) to cover the baseline visible in 90 days of usage — typically 40-60% of total compute spend
- PREFER 1-year over 3-year unless usage has been stable for ≥1 year; 3-year forfeits ~10% extra discount but locks in architecture
- PREFER Compute Savings Plans over EC2 Instance Savings Plans — flexibility across families/regions/Fargate is worth the slightly lower discount
- STACK: Savings Plan covers baseline → Spot covers elastic → On-Demand covers the unpredictable peak
- REVIEW commitment coverage monthly via Cost Explorer — under-utilization means you over-committed, target 95-100% coverage

Trade-offs:
- 3-year commitment: ~28% extra discount vs locked architecture for 3 years
- All Upfront: best discount vs cash-flow impact and worse if you cancel/migrate
- EC2 Instance SP: highest discount but locks family/region — only for very stable workloads

Anti-patterns:
- Buying RIs/Savings Plans before establishing a steady-state baseline — over-committing locks in waste
- Running 100% On-Demand 'because we might change architecture' — leaving 30-50% savings on the table
- Ignoring Savings Plan utilization — under-utilization means you are paying for compute you are not using

metadata.category: Commitments — Savings Plans and Reserved Instances
metadata.title: Savings Plans vs Reserved Instances vs On-Demand mix

text:
NAT Gateway and inter-AZ data transfer cost minimization

Network cost is the most-missed line item. NAT Gateways charge $0.045/hour PLUS $0.045/GB processed, which often exceeds compute cost for chatty workloads. Inter-AZ transfer is $0.01/GB each way. S3 traffic via NAT is the canonical unnecessary cost — VPC endpoints make it free.

Decision rules:
- DEPLOY S3 and DynamoDB Gateway Endpoints in every VPC — free, eliminates NAT charges for S3/DynamoDB traffic
- DEPLOY Interface Endpoints for high-volume AWS services (ECR, CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager) — pays for itself above ~50GB/month
- MINIMIZE inter-AZ chatter — co-locate tightly-coupled services in the same AZ where availability allows (use topology-aware routing in EKS)
- USE VPC Flow Logs + Athena to find top NAT talkers — usually a misconfigured logging or monitoring agent
- AVOID single-AZ NAT for HA — but consider one NAT per AZ to avoid cross-AZ NAT charges (each AZ → its own NAT)

Trade-offs:
- Per-AZ NAT: avoids cross-AZ charges but multiplies hourly fee — usually worth it
- Topology-aware routing: lower cost vs reduced AZ failure tolerance — measure both
- Interface endpoints: ~$7/month/AZ each, breaks even at moderate volume

Anti-patterns:
- All EKS pods in AZ-a calling RDS primary in AZ-b — pays inter-AZ for every read
- S3 backups over NAT instead of via Gateway Endpoint — pure waste
- CloudWatch Logs agent shipping logs over NAT — set up the interface endpoint
- Ignoring data-transfer line item in Cost Explorer — usually 10-30% of total bill

metadata.title: NAT Gateway and inter-AZ data transfer cost minimization

text:
S3 storage tiering, EBS gp3, and RDS sizing

Storage cost compounds silently. S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically and is the safe default for unknown access patterns. EBS gp3 is cheaper than gp2 at equal or better performance and should be the default. RDS instances are commonly over-provisioned for IOPS and storage; Aurora Serverless v2 is the right answer for spiky workloads.

Decision rules:
- USE S3 Intelligent-Tiering as the default storage class for any bucket with mixed/unknown access patterns
- USE S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for compliance archives accessed <1x/quarter; Glacier Deep Archive for never-accessed (>180-day retrieval ok)
- MIGRATE all gp2 EBS volumes to gp3 — same or better perf, ~20% cheaper, no downtime
- USE Aurora Serverless v2 for variable workloads (dev, staging, low-traffic prod); Aurora provisioned for steady high traffic
- ENABLE S3 lifecycle rules to transition logs and backups to cheaper tiers after 30/90/365 days
- RIGHT-SIZE RDS via CloudWatch + Performance Insights — most RDS instances are oversized 2-3x

Trade-offs:
- Intelligent-Tiering: ~$0.0025/1000 objects monitoring fee — not worth it for objects <128KB; for large objects nearly free
- Aurora Serverless v2: scales to zero (in v2, near-zero) vs cold-start latency and per-ACU cost
- Glacier tiers: huge savings vs retrieval cost and latency

Anti-patterns:
- Storing log files in S3 Standard forever — lifecycle them to Glacier or delete
- Provisioned IOPS (io1/io2) on RDS without measured need — gp3 is often sufficient
- Standalone EBS snapshots without lifecycle policy — unbounded growth
- Sizing RDS from the dev guess instead of from CloudWatch — typically 2-3x oversized

metadata.title: S3 storage tiering, EBS gp3, and RDS sizing

text:
Cost-efficient EKS: Karpenter, bin-packing, and resource requests

EKS cost is dominated by the worker nodes, not the control plane. The biggest wins come from (1) accurate pod resource requests so the scheduler bin-packs efficiently, (2) Karpenter for just-in-time, right-sized, Spot-aware node provisioning, and (3) HPA on application metrics, not just CPU.

Decision rules:
- USE Karpenter as the default node provisioner — bin-packs better than Cluster Autoscaler and supports diverse Spot pools
- MEASURE pod requests with VPA recommendation mode for 7+ days before committing — initial guesses are usually 2x off
- RUN HPA on the metric the user cares about (RPS, queue depth) via KEDA, not just CPU
- ENABLE pod priority classes — system pods (CoreDNS, CNI) at high priority, batch jobs at low
- USE Fargate for batch / CI / one-off pods — no node management, pay per pod-second; not for steady traffic

Trade-offs:
- Karpenter: faster scale-up and better bin-packing vs newer than Cluster Autoscaler
- KEDA: scales on real signals vs another component to operate
- Fargate: zero ops vs ~20-30% premium over equivalent EC2

Anti-patterns:
- Running EKS on a single node group of m5.xlarge — no diversity, no bin-packing flexibility
- Setting requests=limits at 4x the actual usage to 'be safe' — destroys cluster economics
- HPA on CPU when the app is I/O bound — pod count grows but throughput does not
- Using Fargate for steady high-traffic workloads — pays the premium without needing the on-demand flexibility

metadata.title: Cost-efficient EKS: Karpenter, bin-packing, and resource requests

text:
Shift-left security and Policy as Code

Integrate security at every SDLC phase: Plan (Threat Modeling), Code (SAST), Build (SCA, Trivy), Test (DAST), Release (SBOM, Snyk), Deploy (Config Audit), Monitor (Runtime Alerts). Use Policy as Code with OPA/Conftest to enforce rules declaratively — e.g. deny if Docker image has no USER or no HEALTHCHECK.

Decision rules:
- Apply security controls at the earliest feasible phase — finding issues in Code is 10x cheaper than in Production
- Express security policies as code (OPA Rego, Conftest) so they are versioned, testable, and automated

Trade-offs:
- Shift-left adds tooling and process overhead in early phases — offset by significantly reducing costly late-stage remediations

Anti-patterns:
- Running security scans only in a pre-production gate — too late in the cycle
- Manual security reviews without automated policy enforcement

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use AWS Config Rules and Security Hub to enforce policies at the infrastructure layer

metadata.title: Shift-left security and Policy as Code

text:
SAST tools for static code security analysis

Recommended SAST tools by language: Semgrep (multi-language, OWASP + custom rules), Bandit (Python, B1xx-B7xx rules: bandit -r ./backend -ll -f json -o bandit-report.json), SpotBugs/FindSec-Bugs (Java), ESLint Security plugin (JS/TS), CodeQL (multi-language, taint tracking). Export results as SARIF for GitHub Security tab integration.

Decision rules:
- Run Semgrep with p/python and p/owasp-top-ten configs as the baseline for Python projects
- Export SARIF format (semgrep --sarif > semgrep.sarif) for GitHub Security tab visibility
- Add CodeQL for deeper taint-tracking analysis on critical codebases

Trade-offs:
- SAST tools generate false positives — tune rules and triage findings before making them pipeline blockers
- CodeQL analysis is slower than Semgrep — run on schedule or PR, not every commit

Anti-patterns:
- Running SAST on test code only — scan production application code
- Suppressing all SAST findings without documented risk acceptance

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Integrate Semgrep SARIF results with Amazon CodeGuru for unified findings

metadata.title: SAST tools for static code security analysis

text:
Secrets management — scan and retrieval best practices

Prevent secrets from entering version control using pre-commit hooks with gitleaks (v8.18.0) and trufflehog (v3.63.0). For runtime secret retrieval in Python, use boto3 to call AWS Secrets Manager get_secret_value — never load secrets from environment variables or config files.

Decision rules:
- Install gitleaks pre-commit hook in every repository to block secret commits before they happen
- Use AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault for runtime secret retrieval — never pass secrets as env vars
- Add trufflehog --only-verified to catch high-confidence secrets that evade simpler regex scanners

Trade-offs:
- Pre-commit hooks only protect developers who have installed them — enforce via CI/CD as a backstop

Anti-patterns:
- Storing secrets in .env files committed to git
- Passing secrets as command-line arguments (visible in process list and shell history)
- Loading secrets from environment variables injected at container startup without a vault

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation for database credentials
- Use Secrets Manager resource policies to restrict secret access to specific IAM roles

metadata.title: Secrets management — scan and retrieval best practices

text:
SBOM generation and vulnerability analysis

Generate a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for every Docker image using Syft (syft myapp:latest -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json). Analyze the SBOM with Grype (grype sbom:./sbom.spdx.json --fail-on high). Alternatively use CycloneDX format (cyclonedx-py environment -o sbom.cyclonedx.json).

Decision rules:
- Generate SBOM in the build stage and store it as a CI artifact alongside the image
- Use grype --fail-on high to block promotion of images with HIGH severity CVEs in dependencies
- Prefer SPDX or CycloneDX formats for tooling interoperability

Trade-offs:
- SBOM generation adds ~30 seconds to the build — acceptable for the supply chain transparency gained

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying images without knowing their dependency inventory
- Not re-scanning SBOMs after new CVEs are published — CVEs are discovered continuously

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Store SBOMs in Amazon S3 alongside image tags for traceability
- Use Amazon Inspector for continuous CVE scanning of ECR images

metadata.title: SBOM generation and vulnerability analysis

text:
Container image signing and verification with Cosign

Sign container images with Cosign (Sigstore): cosign generate-key-pair, cosign sign --key cosign.key myregistry.io/myapp:1.0.0. Verify before deployment: cosign verify --key cosign.pub myregistry.io/myapp:1.0.0. Enforce signature verification in Kubernetes with Kyverno ClusterPolicy (verifyImages).

Decision rules:
- Sign every image pushed to production registry — signing proves the image came from a trusted CI pipeline
- Use Kyverno ClusterPolicy with verifyImages to reject unsigned or untrusted images at admission time

Trade-offs:
- Cosign keyless signing (Fulcio + Rekor) is simpler but requires OIDC identity — good for GitHub Actions
- Key-based signing requires secure storage of the private key (use KMS-backed keys)

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying images from public registries without verifying their provenance
- Using mutable image tags (latest) in production — makes signature verification unreliable

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use AWS Signer for ECR image signing as an alternative to Cosign on EKS

metadata.title: Container image signing and verification with Cosign

text:
Runtime security monitoring with Falco

Use Falco for runtime behavioral detection in containers and Kubernetes. Define custom rules to detect unexpected outbound connections (condition: outbound and not proc.name in allowed_processes). Alerts on anomalies: unexpected shells, file system writes, privilege escalation, data exfiltration patterns.

Decision rules:
- Deploy Falco as a DaemonSet on every Kubernetes node for runtime visibility
- Define an allowlist of expected processes and IPs — alert on any deviation
- Route Falco alerts to SIEM (Splunk, Elasticsearch) or AWS Security Hub for centralized analysis

Trade-offs:
- Falco kernel module/eBPF probe adds small CPU overhead — use eBPF mode for lower overhead
- Default Falco rules generate significant alert volume — tune and create suppression rules for known-good behavior

Anti-patterns:
- Relying solely on pre-deployment scans with no runtime security monitoring
- Running Falco with default rules only without tuning — alert fatigue reduces effectiveness

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use Amazon Security Lake and Amazon Detective for incident investigation of Falco alerts
- GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring is an AWS-managed alternative to Falco on EKS

metadata.title: Runtime security monitoring with Falco

text:
Threat modeling with STRIDE for REST APIs

Apply STRIDE threat model to REST API design: Spoofing (mitigate: JWT/mTLS auth), Tampering (mitigate: HTTPS + request signing), Repudiation (mitigate: immutable audit logs via CloudTrail), Information Disclosure (mitigate: encryption + log filtering), Denial of Service (mitigate: rate limiting + WAF + circuit breakers), Elevation of Privilege (mitigate: RBAC + permission validation per request).

Decision rules:
- Run STRIDE analysis for every new API endpoint or significant feature change
- Map each threat to a concrete control — do not leave any STRIDE category without a mitigation

Trade-offs:
- Threat modeling sessions add time to the design phase — run lightweight threat model reviews (1-2 hours) rather than exhaustive sessions

Anti-patterns:
- Skipping threat modeling and relying entirely on reactive vulnerability scanning
- Treating threat modeling as a one-time exercise — repeat for significant architectural changes

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use AWS Threat Composer as a structured threat modeling tool aligned with AWS services

metadata.title: Threat modeling with STRIDE for REST APIs

text:
DevSecOps checklist by SDLC phase

Phase CODE: pre-commit hooks (secret scan, linting), threat modeling for new features, dependency pinning with hashes. Phase BUILD: SAST (Semgrep, Bandit, CodeQL), SCA (Safety, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check), Dockerfile lint (Hadolint), Docker image scan (Trivy, Grype), SBOM generation. Phase TEST: DAST (OWASP ZAP, Nuclei), auth/authz tests, input fuzzing. Phase DEPLOY: IaC scan (tfsec, Checkov), secrets via Secrets Manager, signed images (Cosign), policy enforcement (OPA/Kyverno). Phase MONITOR: runtime security (Falco), anomaly alerting (GuardDuty, Security Hub), credential rotation, privileged access audit.

Decision rules:
- Treat this checklist as a minimum — automate as many items as possible in CI/CD
- Track checklist completion per release in a security runbook

Trade-offs:
- Automating all checklist items requires significant initial tooling investment — prioritize CODE and BUILD phases first

Anti-patterns:
- Running only one security phase (e.g. SAST only) and skipping others
- Not reviewing checklist after a security incident — update it with lessons learned

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- AWS Security Hub security score tracks many of these controls automatically across AWS services

metadata.title: DevSecOps checklist by SDLC phase

text:
Run containers as non-root (CIS 4.1)

Never run a container as root (UID 0). Create a dedicated user and group in the Dockerfile. Example: groupadd --gid 1001 appgroup && useradd --uid 1001 --gid appgroup --no-create-home appuser, then USER appuser before CMD.

Decision rules:
- Always add a non-root user in the Dockerfile before the CMD/ENTRYPOINT instruction
- Use fixed UID/GID (e.g. 1001) to ensure consistent file ownership across image rebuilds

Trade-offs:
- Some applications require root for initialization — use gosu or tini as entrypoint wrappers to drop privileges after init

Anti-patterns:
- Running containers without a USER directive (defaults to root)
- Using USER root explicitly in production images

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- ECS task definitions should set user in containerDefinitions
- EKS pod specs should set runAsNonRoot: true in securityContext

metadata.title: Run containers as non-root (CIS 4.1)

text:
Read-only container filesystem (CIS 5.12)

Mount the container filesystem as read-only to prevent unauthorized runtime modifications. In docker-compose: read_only: true with tmpfs mounts for /tmp and /var/run. CLI equivalent: docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapp:latest.

Decision rules:
- Enable read_only: true for all stateless services
- Add tmpfs mounts for directories requiring write access at runtime (e.g. /tmp, /var/run)

Trade-offs:
- Application must not write to the container filesystem — may require refactoring logging or temp file paths

Anti-patterns:
- Running containers with writable root filesystem in production
- Not providing tmpfs for required write paths when read-only is enabled

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Map to readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in ECS containerDefinitions
- Map to readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in Kubernetes securityContext

metadata.title: Read-only container filesystem (CIS 5.12)

text:
Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities (CIS 5.3)

Start by dropping all Linux capabilities (cap_drop: ALL), then add back only those strictly required (e.g. cap_add: NET_BIND_SERVICE if the service listens on a port below 1024).

Decision rules:
- Apply cap_drop: [ALL] as the baseline for every container
- Add back only specific capabilities required by the application — document the reason

Trade-offs:
- Identifying required capabilities may take experimentation; run container with strace or auditd to detect capability use

Anti-patterns:
- Running containers without capability restrictions
- Adding broad capabilities (SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN) without justification

metadata.title: Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities (CIS 5.3)

text:
Enforce resource limits (CIS 5.10 / 5.11)

Always define memory and CPU limits to prevent a single container from causing Denial of Service. In docker-compose deploy.resources: limits memory 512m cpus 0.5, reservations memory 128m cpus 0.1.

Decision rules:
- Set both memory limits and CPU limits for all production containers
- Define reservations (requests) in addition to limits to enable proper scheduling

Trade-offs:
- Limits that are too tight cause OOM kills or CPU throttling — profile the application before setting values

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying containers with no memory or CPU limits to shared hosts
- Setting limits without reservations — scheduler cannot guarantee resource availability

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Map to memory and cpu in ECS task definition resource requirements
- Map to resources.requests and resources.limits in Kubernetes pod spec

metadata.title: Enforce resource limits (CIS 5.10 / 5.11)

text:
Disable privileged mode (CIS 5.4)

Never use privileged: true in production. Privileged containers have full access to the host kernel. Use security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true] to prevent privilege escalation.

Decision rules:
- Set security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true] on all containers
- Reject any deployment manifest that sets privileged: true without explicit documented justification

Trade-offs:
- Some monitoring or networking tools require privileged mode — isolate them in dedicated namespaces with extra controls

Anti-patterns:
- Setting privileged: true for application containers
- Using privileged mode as a workaround for missing capabilities

metadata.title: Disable privileged mode (CIS 5.4)

text:
Apply Seccomp and AppArmor profiles (CIS 5.1 / 5.2)

Attach a seccomp profile (seccomp:seccomp-profile.json) and AppArmor profile (apparmor:docker-default) via security_opt to restrict the system calls available to the container.

Decision rules:
- Use the docker-default AppArmor profile as a minimum baseline
- Use the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile in Kubernetes (seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault)

Trade-offs:
- Custom seccomp profiles require profiling the application's syscall usage first
- AppArmor is Linux-specific — not applicable on Windows containers

Anti-patterns:
- Running containers with unconfined seccomp (--security-opt seccomp=unconfined)
- Disabling AppArmor profiles for production containers

metadata.title: Apply Seccomp and AppArmor profiles (CIS 5.1 / 5.2)

text:
Use minimal base images to reduce attack surface

Prefer distroless (no shell, no package manager) or alpine (~5 MB) base images. Distroless example: gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12. Alpine example: python:3.11-alpine. Fewer packages means fewer CVEs.

Decision rules:
- Default to *-slim variants when distroless is not feasible
- Use distroless for production runtime stages in multi-stage builds
- Run image scanners after every build to detect new CVEs

Trade-offs:
- Distroless images have no shell — debugging requires ephemeral debug containers (kubectl debug)
- Alpine uses musl libc — some Python packages may not have compatible wheels

Anti-patterns:
- Using ubuntu:latest or debian:latest as a base image for production containers
- Not updating base images regularly — stale images accumulate CVEs

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- ECR image scanning with Snyk/Trivy should be enabled for all repositories

metadata.title: Use minimal base images to reduce attack surface

text:
Scan images for vulnerabilities before deployment

Use vulnerability scanners on every image before pushing or deploying. Tools: Trivy (trivy image myapp:latest --severity CRITICAL,HIGH), Grype (grype myapp:latest), Docker Scout (docker scout cves myapp:latest).

Decision rules:
- Gate CI/CD pipeline on Trivy or Grype scan results — fail on CRITICAL severity
- Scan both the application image and the base image separately

Trade-offs:
- Scanning adds 1-5 minutes to CI pipeline — acceptable for security assurance
- Scanners may produce false positives — triage HIGH findings before blocking

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying images without any vulnerability scan
- Ignoring CRITICAL CVEs in scanner output without documented risk acceptance

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Enable Amazon ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector-based) for automatic push-time scanning

metadata.title: Scan images for vulnerabilities before deployment

text:
Never embed secrets in Docker images (CIS 4.10)

Do not use ENV to set secrets (e.g. ENV API_KEY=sk-secret123). Use Docker BuildKit secrets (RUN --mount=type=secret,id=api_key) or inject secrets at runtime via environment variables from a vault or secrets manager.

Decision rules:
- Reject any Dockerfile with ENV instructions containing passwords, tokens, or API keys
- Use RUN --mount=type=secret for secrets needed only during build time (e.g. pip install from private registry)

Trade-offs:
- BuildKit secret mounts require Docker BuildKit enabled (DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1)

Anti-patterns:
- ENV API_KEY=sk-secret123 in Dockerfile — secret is visible in image history
- ARG SECRET=default_value — visible in build logs and image metadata

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Inject secrets from AWS Secrets Manager at container startup via ECS secrets configuration
- Use Parameter Store or Secrets Manager references in ECS task definitions

metadata.title: Never embed secrets in Docker images (CIS 4.10)

text:
Use .dockerignore to exclude sensitive files

A comprehensive .dockerignore prevents secrets and unnecessary files from being added to the build context. Should exclude: .env, .env.*, *.pem, *.key, *.p12, secrets/, .git/, __pycache__/, *.pyc, node_modules/, .DS_Store.

Decision rules:
- Always include a .dockerignore in every project with a Dockerfile
- Exclude all secret files, credentials, and VCS metadata from the build context

Trade-offs:
- Over-aggressive .dockerignore may exclude files needed for the build — review carefully

Anti-patterns:
- Not having a .dockerignore — risks accidentally copying .env or private keys into the image
- Copying the entire repository context without filtering out secrets

metadata.title: Use .dockerignore to exclude sensitive files

text:
Python FastAPI multi-stage Dockerfile with non-root user and health check

Two-stage Python production Dockerfile: builder stage (python:3.11-slim) installs packages with pip install --no-cache-dir --user, runtime stage (python:3.11-slim) creates non-root appuser (UID 1001), copies /root/.local from builder, sets PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, adds HEALTHCHECK with httpx, exposes 8000. CMD: uvicorn with --workers 1 --no-access-log.

Decision rules:
- Use --user flag in pip install to install to /root/.local, then copy to the runtime user's home
- Set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 to skip .pyc file generation in the runtime image
- Add HEALTHCHECK with initialDelaySeconds=40s to accommodate application startup time

Trade-offs:
- Runtime stage still uses python:3.11-slim (not distroless) to allow httpx for health check — use distroless if health check is done via external probe

Anti-patterns:
- Installing dependencies in the runtime stage — defeats the multi-stage cache benefit
- Running uvicorn with multiple workers behind a container orchestrator — use 1 worker per container and scale horizontally

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Map HEALTHCHECK to ECS container health check for load balancer target group deregistration

metadata.title: Python FastAPI multi-stage Dockerfile with non-root user and health check

text:
Node.js multi-stage Dockerfile with npm ci and non-root user

Two-stage Node.js Dockerfile: builder stage (node:20-alpine) runs npm ci --only=production and npm run build, runtime stage (node:20-alpine) creates non-root appuser (UID 1001), copies dist and node_modules with --chown, adds HEALTHCHECK with wget, exposes 3000. CMD: node dist/server.js.

Decision rules:
- Use npm ci (not npm install) in builder stage — deterministic install from package-lock.json
- Use --only=production in npm ci to exclude devDependencies from the runtime image
- Use alpine variant to minimize image size

Trade-offs:
- Alpine uses musl libc — some native Node.js addons may have compatibility issues; use debian-slim variants if needed

Anti-patterns:
- Using npm install instead of npm ci — non-deterministic and slower
- Copying node_modules from host into the image — includes devDependencies and platform-specific binaries

metadata.title: Node.js multi-stage Dockerfile with npm ci and non-root user

text:
Java Spring Boot multi-stage Dockerfile with layer extraction

Two-stage Spring Boot Dockerfile: builder stage (maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17) runs mvn dependency:go-offline -B to cache deps, then mvn package -DskipTests -B. Runtime stage (eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine) creates non-root appuser, runs java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract to split JAR into layers for better Docker caching, adds HEALTHCHECK with wget on /actuator/health. JVM options: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0, -XX:+UseContainerSupport.

Decision rules:
- Run mvn dependency:go-offline before copying src — creates a cacheable layer for Maven dependencies
- Use -Djarmode=layertools to extract Spring Boot layers for optimized Docker caching on partial rebuilds
- Use -XX:UseContainerSupport and -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 for proper JVM memory management in containers

Trade-offs:
- Layer extraction increases build steps but significantly reduces rebuild time when only application code changes

Anti-patterns:
- Copying all Maven dependencies into the final image — use the JRE runtime stage only
- Not setting -XX:UseContainerSupport — JVM may use host memory limits instead of container limits, causing OOMKills

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Set JVM MaxRAMPercentage to leave headroom for the container memory limit overhead in ECS/EKS

metadata.title: Java Spring Boot multi-stage Dockerfile with layer extraction

text:
Comprehensive .dockerignore template

Exclude from Docker build context: version control (.git/, .gitignore, .gitattributes), secrets (.env, .env.*, *.pem, *.key, *.p12, *.pfx, secrets/), Python artifacts (__pycache__/, *.pyc, .venv/, dist/, .pytest_cache/, .mypy_cache/, htmlcov/), Node artifacts (node_modules/, npm-debug.log, .npm/), Docker files (Dockerfile*, docker-compose*, .dockerignore), IDE files (.idea/, .vscode/, .DS_Store), CI/CD files (.github/, Jenkinsfile), docs (docs/, *.md), tests (tests/, test/, spec/).

Decision rules:
- Always include a .dockerignore in every project that has a Dockerfile
- Exclude .env* patterns to prevent accidental secret inclusion in build context
- Exclude tests/ to keep production images smaller

Trade-offs:
- Excluding Dockerfile and docker-compose files from context is safe but may complicate multi-stage builds that copy compose files — adjust as needed

Anti-patterns:
- Not having a .dockerignore — entire repository including secrets is sent to Docker daemon
- Using COPY . . without a .dockerignore

metadata.title: Comprehensive .dockerignore template

text:
Docker layer cache optimization strategy

Optimize Docker build cache by separating frequently changing layers from stable layers. Pattern: COPY requirements.txt . (stable — cache hit), RUN pip install -r requirements.txt (cached unless requirements change), COPY . . (frequently changing — always invalidates). The wrong pattern copies all source before installing, invalidating the pip install cache on every code change.

Decision rules:
- Always copy dependency manifests (requirements.txt, package.json, pom.xml) before copying source code
- Place COPY . . as late as possible in the Dockerfile to maximize cache reuse of earlier layers

Trade-offs:
- Separate dependency and source COPY instructions add a line to the Dockerfile but dramatically reduce CI build times

Anti-patterns:
- COPY . . followed by RUN pip install — invalidates pip cache on every code change
- Combining dependency installation and source copy in a single RUN — prevents cache layering

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use GitHub Actions cache with type=gha for Docker BuildKit layer caching in CI (cache-from/cache-to gha)

metadata.title: Docker layer cache optimization strategy

text:
Generic Backend + Redis Docker Compose

Compose pattern for a generic backend service with Redis 7. Backend receives REDIS_URL from environment and depends_on redis. Redis uses redis:7 official image and publishes port 6379. REDIS_URL format for this compose: redis://redis:6379.

Decision rules:
- Use when the backend requires Redis for caching, rate limiting, queuing, or session storage
- Set REDIS_URL to redis://redis:6379 to use the compose service name as hostname

Trade-offs:
- No Redis persistence (no appendonly or named volume) — data lost on container restart
- No Redis authentication — add requirepass via command: redis-server --requirepass ... for non-dev environments

Anti-patterns:
- Do not run Redis without authentication in staging or production
- Do not expose port 6379 to external networks

metadata.title: Generic Backend + Redis Docker Compose

text:
FastAPI + PostgreSQL Docker Compose Pattern

Docker Compose pattern for a FastAPI backend with a PostgreSQL 15 database. Backend service builds from Dockerfile, maps port 8000:8000, receives DATABASE_URL from environment, depends_on db. DB service uses postgres:15 official image with POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB from env vars, publishes port 5432.

Decision rules:
- Use for local development and integration testing of FastAPI + PostgreSQL stacks
- Credentials must be passed via .env file — never hardcoded in docker-compose.yml
- Use depends_on to control startup order (does not wait for DB readiness — add healthcheck for that)

Trade-offs:
- No named volume for db service — data is lost on docker-compose down; add volumes for persistence
- No healthcheck on db — backend may attempt connections before PostgreSQL is fully ready

Anti-patterns:
- Do not hardcode POSTGRES_PASSWORD in docker-compose.yml
- Do not publish port 5432 to 0.0.0.0 in production or shared environments

metadata.title: FastAPI + PostgreSQL Docker Compose Pattern

text:
Full-stack FastAPI + Streamlit + PostgreSQL Compose

Compose pattern for a three-service stack: FastAPI backend (port 8000) receiving DATABASE_URL and GROQ_API_KEY, Streamlit frontend (port 8501) depending on backend, and PostgreSQL 15 database. Frontend overrides CMD to run streamlit. All credentials supplied via environment variables.

Decision rules:
- Use for full-stack Python applications with Streamlit UI, FastAPI API, and PostgreSQL
- Frontend depends_on backend — Compose starts backend service first
- Pass GROQ_API_KEY and other third-party API keys only via .env or Docker secrets

Trade-offs:
- No persistent volume for database — add a named volume under volumes: for data durability
- No readiness healthchecks — services may connect before dependencies finish initializing

Anti-patterns:
- Do not hardcode API keys (e.g. GROQ_API_KEY) inline in docker-compose.yml
- Do not expose all internal service ports to the host unnecessarily

metadata.title: Full-stack FastAPI + Streamlit + PostgreSQL Compose

text:
Spring Boot + MySQL Docker Compose

Compose pattern for Spring Boot backend (port 8080) with MySQL 8.0 database (port 3306). Both services receive MYSQL_DATABASE, MYSQL_USER, MYSQL_PASSWORD, MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD from environment. Backend depends_on db.

Decision rules:
- Use when language=java, framework=spring_boot, dependencies include mysql
- MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD is required for MySQL 8.0 container initialization even when a regular user is defined

Trade-offs:
- No persistent volume — MySQL data is lost on container removal; add a named volume for durability
- No healthcheck on db — Spring Boot may attempt JDBC connections before MySQL is accepting them

Anti-patterns:
