- Do not hardcode MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD or MYSQL_PASSWORD in the compose file
- Do not expose port 3306 to 0.0.0.0 in internet-facing environments

metadata.title: Spring Boot + MySQL Docker Compose

text:
FastAPI PostgreSQL-backed Dockerfile

FastAPI Dockerfile aligned with a PostgreSQL-backed service. Base image: python:3.11-slim. Installs pip requirements, sets ENV PORT=8000, exposes 8000. CMD uses ${PORT:-8000} for configurable port binding at runtime.

Decision rules:
- Use when framework=fastapi, project_type=api_backend, dependencies include postgres
- Use PORT env variable to allow dynamic port assignment in orchestration environments

Trade-offs:
- No multi-stage build — simpler but larger final image than a distroless multi-stage variant
- No non-root user — extend with USER directive before CMD for production security

Anti-patterns:
- Do not embed DATABASE_URL or credentials in the Dockerfile
- Do not expose the database port inside the application container Dockerfile

metadata.title: FastAPI PostgreSQL-backed Dockerfile

text:
FastAPI Uvicorn Minimal Dockerfile

Minimal Dockerfile for a FastAPI backend started with uvicorn. Base image: python:3.11-slim. WORKDIR /app. Copies requirements.txt first, runs pip install --no-cache-dir, then copies full source. Sets PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, exposes port 8000. CMD: sh -c uvicorn backend.app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000.

Decision rules:
- Use when project_type=api_backend, framework=fastapi, runtime=pip
- Use python:3.11-slim to keep image size minimal
- Set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 so log output is streamed immediately to stdout

Trade-offs:
- No multi-stage build — image includes pip and build tools, larger than distroless variants
- No non-root USER defined — extend with USER directive for production hardening

Anti-patterns:
- Do not hardcode secrets in ENV or ARG instructions inside the Dockerfile
- Do not COPY . . before COPY requirements.txt — breaks Docker layer caching

metadata.title: FastAPI Uvicorn Minimal Dockerfile

text:
Generic Python Backend Dockerfile

Simple fallback Dockerfile for a Python backend service when no specialized framework (FastAPI, Flask, Streamlit) is detected. Base: python:3.11-slim. Installs pip requirements, copies source. Sets PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1. CMD: sh -c python main.py.

Decision rules:
- Use when language=python, framework=generic, project_type=backend_service
- Fall back to this template only when no framework-specific Dockerfile exists

Trade-offs:
- Assumes main.py as entrypoint — must be updated if the entrypoint differs
- No multi-stage build and no non-root user — extend for production hardening

Anti-patterns:
- Do not use python:latest — always pin to a specific version (e.g. python:3.11-slim)
- Do not copy source before installing requirements — always install deps first

metadata.title: Generic Python Backend Dockerfile

text:
Spring Boot Maven Multi-stage Dockerfile

Multi-stage Dockerfile for a Spring Boot service built with Maven. Build stage: maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 — copies pom.xml and mvnw, runs mvnw -DskipTests package. Runtime stage: eclipse-temurin:17-jre — copies compiled JAR, exposes 8080, ENTRYPOINT java -jar /app/app.jar.

Decision rules:
- Use when language=java, framework=spring_boot, runtime=maven
- Multi-stage separates build tools from the runtime image, significantly reducing final image size
- Use eclipse-temurin:17-jre (JRE only, not JDK) in runtime stage

Trade-offs:
- Build time is longer due to Maven dependency resolution, mitigated by caching pom.xml separately
- mvnw wrapper must exist in project root; fall back to mvn if absent

Anti-patterns:
- Do not use a JDK image in the runtime stage — use JRE to minimize attack surface
- Do not skip -DskipTests if test failures should gate the build

metadata.title: Spring Boot Maven Multi-stage Dockerfile

text:
Spring Boot MySQL Dockerfile

Multi-stage Dockerfile for Spring Boot with MySQL. Build stage: maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17. Runtime stage: eclipse-temurin:17-jre. Supports JAVA_OPTS env variable for JVM tuning. ENTRYPOINT uses sh -c to expand $JAVA_OPTS at container startup.

Decision rules:
- Use when language=java, framework=spring_boot, dependencies include mysql
- JAVA_OPTS pattern allows tuning heap/GC flags without rebuilding the image

Trade-offs:
- sh -c entrypoint adds a shell process but enables env var expansion in JAVA_OPTS
- No non-root user defined — add USER directive before ENTRYPOINT for production hardening

Anti-patterns:
- Do not hardcode MYSQL_PASSWORD or connection URL in the Dockerfile
- Do not use a JDK image in the runtime stage

metadata.title: Spring Boot MySQL Dockerfile

text:
Streamlit Web UI Dockerfile

Dockerfile for a Streamlit web UI service. Base: python:3.11-slim. Installs pip requirements, copies source, exposes port 8501. CMD: streamlit run frontend/app.py --server.port 8501 --server.address 0.0.0.0.

Decision rules:
- Use when framework=streamlit, project_type=web_ui
- Always bind to --server.address 0.0.0.0 (not 127.0.0.1) so the container port is reachable externally
- Default Streamlit port is 8501 — map to desired host port in docker-compose or Kubernetes

Trade-offs:
- Single-stage build — suitable for frontend UI services where image size is less critical
- No non-root user — add USER directive for security-hardened deployments

Anti-patterns:
- Do not bind to 127.0.0.1 (localhost) inside the container — traffic will not reach the service
- Do not hardcode --server.port if flexible port binding across environments is needed

metadata.title: Streamlit Web UI Dockerfile

text:
Generic External API .env.example Template

Safe .env.example for backend services integrating with external APIs. Empty placeholders for API_BASE_URL (base URL of the external service) and API_KEY (authentication token). Generic template applicable to any third-party REST API.

Decision rules:
- Use API_BASE_URL to allow URL switching between sandbox and production endpoints
- Prefer bearer token (API_KEY) over username/password credentials for API authentication

Anti-patterns:
- Never hardcode API keys in source code or Dockerfiles
- Do not reuse a single API key across multiple services — provision separate keys per service

metadata.title: Generic External API .env.example Template

text:
FastAPI PostgreSQL .env.example Template

Safe .env.example template for FastAPI with PostgreSQL. Defines empty placeholders for DATABASE_URL (SQLAlchemy connection string), POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB. All values intentionally blank to avoid committing credentials.

Decision rules:
- Commit .env.example to version control; never commit a populated .env file
- DATABASE_URL format for SQLAlchemy: postgresql+asyncpg://user:password@host:5432/dbname
- POSTGRES_* vars are consumed directly by the postgres:15 Docker image for initialization

Anti-patterns:
- Never set default values in .env.example — blanks are intentional
- Never commit .env files with real credentials or tokens to version control

metadata.title: FastAPI PostgreSQL .env.example Template

text:
Spring Boot MySQL .env.example Template

Safe .env.example for Spring Boot with MySQL. Empty placeholders for MYSQL_DATABASE, MYSQL_USER, MYSQL_PASSWORD, MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD. All values blank to prevent credential leakage.

Decision rules:
- MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD is required by MySQL 8.0 container during initialization even when a regular user is also defined
- Inject real values via CI/CD pipeline secrets (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables, etc.) or a vault

Anti-patterns:
- Never set default passwords in .env.example
- Never commit a populated .env file — use .gitignore to exclude .env

metadata.title: Spring Boot MySQL .env.example Template

text:
Users vs Roles vs Federated Identity

IAM users are long-lived credentials and should be the exception, not the rule. Roles are short-lived assumed credentials issued by STS and are the correct primitive for workloads, cross-account access, and human SSO. Federated identity (IAM Identity Center / SSO with SAML or OIDC) replaces IAM users for human access. The identity model decides everything downstream: rotation, audit, blast radius.

Decision rules:
- USE IAM Identity Center (SSO) for all human access — federated, MFA-enforced, group-mapped, no static keys
- USE IAM roles for all workloads (EC2 instance profile, ECS task role, EKS IRSA, Lambda execution role)
- AVOID creating IAM users except for: (a) emergency break-glass, (b) third-party tools that cannot federate
- ROTATE any unavoidable IAM access keys every 90 days max; alert on keys older than 180 days
- REQUIRE MFA on all IAM users and on the root account; root credentials must be vaulted and never used for daily ops

Trade-offs:
- Roles + STS: ephemeral and audited but require trust-policy management and assume-role boilerplate
- IAM Identity Center: centralized but adds a dependency on AWS Organizations and SSO config
- Long-lived users: simple but high blast radius on credential leak

Anti-patterns:
- Embedding IAM access keys in CI variables or Dockerfiles — use OIDC federation to AWS instead
- Sharing IAM users between humans — destroys audit trail
- Using the root account for any operation other than billing and account-level setup
- Creating one IAM role per service AND attaching AdministratorAccess as a 'temporary' fix

metadata.title: Users vs Roles vs Federated Identity

text:
Writing least-privilege policies that survive review

Least privilege means starting from zero permissions and adding only what is provably required. Production policies must scope by Action, Resource, and Condition. Wildcards in Resource are the single largest source of accidental privilege escalation. AWS provides Access Analyzer (Policy Generation) which generates policies from CloudTrail history — the recommended starting point for any non-trivial role.

Decision rules:
- GENERATE candidate policies with IAM Access Analyzer Policy Generation from 90 days of CloudTrail
- SCOPE every Action to specific Resource ARNs — `Resource: "*"` is allowed only for genuinely global APIs (e.g. ec2:DescribeRegions)
- USE Conditions for defense-in-depth: aws:SourceVpc, aws:SourceIp, aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:RequestTag
- USE permission boundaries on roles created by developers — boundary caps the maximum reachable privilege
- DENY wins — use explicit Deny statements as guardrails (e.g. deny iam:* outside a specific admin role)
- TAG roles and use ABAC (`aws:ResourceTag/Project`) for multi-team accounts to keep policies short

Trade-offs:
- Strict scoping: high security but more policy churn when new resources appear — mitigate with ABAC
- Permission boundaries: protect against privilege escalation but add cognitive load for engineers
- Service Control Policies (SCPs) at the org level: blunt but powerful guardrail vs per-account complexity

Anti-patterns:
- `Action: "*", Resource: "*"` — that is AdministratorAccess by another name
- Attaching `*FullAccess` AWS-managed policies to workload roles — they are too broad for production
- Using `iam:PassRole` with `Resource: "*"` — enables privilege escalation via Lambda/EC2/ECS
- Skipping Conditions — a policy without `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:PrincipalOrgID` is exploitable from any account that gets the credentials

metadata.title: Writing least-privilege policies that survive review

text:
AssumeRole with ExternalId for third-party and cross-account

Cross-account access is implemented with an IAM role in the target account whose trust policy permits a principal in a different account (or third-party AWS account) to call sts:AssumeRole. For third-party access, the trust policy MUST require an `sts:ExternalId` known only to the third party — this prevents the confused-deputy attack where another customer of the same vendor could assume your role.

Decision rules:
- REQUIRE sts:ExternalId in the trust policy of any role assumable by a third-party AWS account
- GENERATE a unique, high-entropy ExternalId per integration; never reuse across customers or roles
- SCOPE the trust policy Principal to a specific account ID, not aws:PrincipalOrgID, when integrating with vendors
- USE aws:PrincipalOrgID in trust policies for INTRA-organization access — it auto-trusts all member accounts
- SET role session duration to the minimum that completes the job (default 1h, max 12h)
- LOG all sts:AssumeRole calls and alert on unexpected source accounts

Trade-offs:
- Short session duration: better security vs more refresh churn for long-running jobs
- PrincipalOrgID trust: scales with org growth but trusts every account — pair with SCPs
- Per-vendor unique role: clean blast radius vs more roles to manage

Anti-patterns:
- Trust policy with `Principal: "*"` — any AWS account in the world can assume the role
- Reusing the same ExternalId across multiple vendors — defeats the confused-deputy mitigation
- Granting cross-account access by sharing IAM access keys instead of using AssumeRole
- Allowing the role to call sts:AssumeRole on itself or a more privileged role (chained escalation)

metadata.title: AssumeRole with ExternalId for third-party and cross-account

text:
IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) on EKS

IRSA binds a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to an IAM role via OIDC federation. Pods using that ServiceAccount receive short-lived, automatically-rotated AWS credentials with exactly the role's permissions. IRSA replaces the older anti-patterns of (a) attaching IAM permissions to the entire node, and (b) baking access keys into pods. It is the only correct way to give a pod AWS access in production.

Decision rules:
- ENABLE the cluster OIDC provider and create per-application IAM roles bound to per-application ServiceAccounts
- SCOPE the role's trust policy to the exact `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>` subject — not the whole cluster
- STRIP node-level IAM permissions to the absolute minimum (ECR pull, CNI, autoscaler) — never put app permissions on the node role
- USE one role per workload — never share an IRSA role across distinct applications or namespaces
- PAIR IRSA with NetworkPolicy and PodSecurityStandard restricted — IRSA only covers AWS API access, not in-cluster access

Trade-offs:
- Per-workload roles: clean blast radius vs more roles and trust policies to manage (Terraform module helps)
- IRSA: cleanest workload identity vs requires OIDC provider setup; alternative is Pod Identity (newer, simpler)
- EKS Pod Identity (2023+): simpler than IRSA, no OIDC required, but cluster-scoped agent dependency

Anti-patterns:
- Attaching application-specific IAM permissions to the node IAM role — every pod on the node inherits them
- Mounting AWS credentials as a Kubernetes Secret — long-lived, no automatic rotation
- Using a single 'app' ServiceAccount across all workloads — defeats per-workload least privilege
- Trust policy with subject claim `system:serviceaccount:*:*` — any pod in the cluster can assume the role

metadata.title: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) on EKS

text:
IAM monitoring, anomaly detection, and key compromise response

Even a perfect policy can be defeated by a stolen credential. Production accounts must continuously monitor for suspicious IAM activity and have a rehearsed compromise-response playbook. AWS GuardDuty produces high-fidelity findings (CredentialAccess, Discovery, Persistence) and Access Analyzer surfaces external access and unused permissions.

Decision rules:
- ENABLE GuardDuty in all accounts and regions; route findings to Security Hub and a SIEM
- ENABLE IAM Access Analyzer (external access + unused access); review unused permissions quarterly
- ENABLE CloudTrail (org trail, multi-region, log file validation, S3 with object lock)
- ALERT on: root login, MFA disable, IAM user creation, access key creation, AssumeRole from a new source IP/ASN, console login without MFA
- ROTATE on compromise: deactivate the credential, invalidate all sessions (sts:RevokeOlderSessions), audit CloudTrail for actions taken with the credential
- PRACTICE the runbook quarterly — credential compromise drills surface gaps before incidents

Trade-offs:
- GuardDuty: high signal but ~$1-5/account/day baseline; turn on in every account anyway
- Aggressive alerting: catches real incidents but generates noise — tune in the first 30 days
- Session revocation: fast containment but can disrupt ongoing legitimate work

Anti-patterns:
- Treating a leaked access key as 'just rotate the key' — the attacker may have created backdoor users, roles, or trust policies in the meantime
- Disabling CloudTrail in dev accounts to save cost — those accounts are the easiest pivot point into prod
- No alerting on root account use — root use should be vanishingly rare and always investigated
- Storing CloudTrail logs in the same account being audited — an attacker with admin can delete them

metadata.title: IAM monitoring, anomaly detection, and key compromise response

text:
Public S3 bucket leaks customer data

A developer creates an S3 bucket for a one-off export, sets ACL to public-read 'just to share with the partner', forgets to revert it. A bucket-enumeration scanner finds it weeks later. The file contains PII or credentials. This is the most common cloud data-leak pattern in public DBIR data and continues to dominate cloud breaches in 2024-2025.

Preventive controls:
- Enable S3 Block Public Access at the ACCOUNT level — overrides any bucket-level setting
- Enable S3 Block Public Access at the ORGANIZATION level via SCP — even break-glass admins cannot toggle off
- Default encryption with KMS CMK — even on accidental public exposure, the object is encrypted
- Use IAM Access Analyzer for S3 — flags any bucket reachable from outside the org
- Use bucket policies that explicitly deny `s3:GetObject` when `aws:PrincipalOrgID` does not match

Detection signals:
- Access Analyzer finding 'External access granted to bucket'
- GuardDuty finding `Discovery:S3/MaliciousIPCaller.Custom`
- CloudTrail `PutBucketAcl` or `PutBucketPolicy` events outside the change-management window
- Macie sensitive-data discovery on a bucket newly flagged public

Remediation runbook:
1. Immediately make bucket private (set ACL private, attach explicit deny policy)
2. Enumerate access via S3 server access logs and CloudFront logs (if fronted)
3. Identify objects accessed and notify per breach-disclosure obligations
4. Rotate any credentials, tokens, or keys present in the leaked objects
5. Add the bucket to weekly Access Analyzer review until permanently retired

Anti-patterns:
- Relying on bucket-level Block Public Access only — account-level is the right layer
- Treating 'private bucket with a presigned URL' as the same as a public bucket — presigned URLs in logs/Slack are a separate exposure class
- Not enabling S3 server access logs — without them, breach scope cannot be determined

metadata.title: Public S3 bucket leaks customer data

text:
Application SSRF reaches IMDS and steals instance role credentials (Capital One 2019 pattern)

An application has an SSRF vulnerability (often via image-fetch or webhook validation). Attacker forces the app to GET http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>. IMDSv1 returns role credentials. Attacker uses them to enumerate and exfiltrate S3 data. This is the Capital One 2019 pattern — 100M records, $190M total cost.

Preventive controls:
- ENFORCE IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) on every instance and launch template — IMDSv2 requires a session token that SSRF cannot easily acquire
- BLOCK PUT to /latest/api/token in WAF/proxy and SET IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 (default 2) for non-containerized workloads
- USE IRSA in EKS (no IMDS exposure to pods) — pods get credentials via projected SA token, not metadata service
- MINIMIZE the role attached to compute — SSRF stealing a role with `s3:Get*` on one bucket is incident-class lower than stealing AdministratorAccess
- USE VPC endpoint policies and SG egress rules to limit where stolen credentials can be used FROM (less effective but layered)

Detection signals:
- GuardDuty `UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS`
- CloudTrail `AssumeRole` or API calls from the instance role with sourceIPAddress outside the expected VPC NAT range
- Sudden spike in `s3:ListBuckets` or `s3:GetObject` from an instance role
- WAF logs showing requests to internal IPs (169.254.x.x) in URL parameters

Remediation runbook:
1. Revoke active sessions: `aws iam put-role-policy` with a deny-all + condition `aws:TokenIssueTime` < now
2. Patch the SSRF vulnerability (input validation, internal-IP blocklist, IMDSv2)
3. Audit CloudTrail for the credential's actions — every API call with the stolen credential
4. Rotate any data accessed (re-encrypt with new KMS key)
5. Review and minimize the instance role permissions

Anti-patterns:
- Allowing IMDSv1 for backward compatibility — SSRF defeats it trivially
- Granting compute roles broad S3 access ('AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess') — turns SSRF from incident into breach
- Application-level SSRF allowlist by hostname only — DNS rebinding bypasses it

metadata.title: Application SSRF reaches IMDS and steals instance role credentials (Capital One 2019 pattern)

text:
Public Kubernetes dashboard or unauthenticated kubelet leads to cluster takeover (Tesla 2018 pattern)

An admin exposes the Kubernetes dashboard via a LoadBalancer service for convenience, with anonymous-auth enabled or no authentication. Attacker reaches it, deploys a cryptominer or pivots into the cluster. Tesla's 2018 incident (cryptojacking via exposed Kubernetes dashboard) is the canonical case. Kubelet read-only port (10255) and unauthenticated API server present similar risks.

Preventive controls:
- NEVER expose the Kubernetes dashboard publicly — port-forward or behind SSO/identity-aware proxy only
- DISABLE anonymous auth on the API server (`--anonymous-auth=false`) and on kubelet (`--anonymous-auth=false`)
- DISABLE the kubelet read-only port (`--read-only-port=0`)
- RESTRICT API server access via SG / authorized networks — public API endpoint should be IP-allowlisted in EKS
- ENFORCE PodSecurityStandard `restricted` in every namespace except kube-system

Detection signals:
- GuardDuty for EKS Runtime Monitoring findings (`CryptoCurrency:Runtime/BitcoinTool.B`)
- Unexpected new namespace, Deployment, or DaemonSet in audit logs
- Outbound network traffic to known mining pools (Falco rule)
- `kubectl auth can-i --as=system:anonymous` returning yes for any verb

Remediation runbook:
1. Rotate cluster admin credentials, all ServiceAccount tokens, and any cloud credentials reachable from the cluster
2. Audit all workloads for unknown images, init containers, and recently-added DaemonSets
3. Inspect node-level processes (Falco / runtime detection) for resident malware
4. Rebuild compromised nodes — assume node OS compromise

Anti-patterns:
- Exposing the dashboard 'temporarily' for a demo — it never gets removed
- Treating private subnets as enough — one compromised pod inside the cluster reaches the dashboard too
- kubectl proxy in a long-running tmux session — a stolen laptop gives cluster-admin

metadata.title: Public Kubernetes dashboard or unauthenticated kubelet leads to cluster takeover (Tesla 2018 pattern)

text:
AWS access key committed to public repo (or even private repo with broad access)

Developer commits `.env` or hardcoded key, pushes to GitHub. Within minutes (literally — there are bots scanning new commits), the key is found and used to spin up crypto-mining instances or exfiltrate data. Even private repos are not safe: a contractor with read access, a leaked PAT, or accidental fork can leak the secret.

Preventive controls:
- PRE-COMMIT hooks: gitleaks or trufflehog blocking commits containing key patterns
- GITHUB push protection (free tier as of 2024) — server-side block of detected secrets
- ELIMINATE long-lived keys: use OIDC federation from CI to AWS instead of static keys
- SCAN repos continuously (gitleaks-action, GitHub secret scanning) — secrets predate push protection
- Rotate any committed secret IMMEDIATELY — assume it leaked even if you force-pushed it away. Git history is forever in clones and forks.

Detection signals:
- GitHub secret-scanning alert
- GuardDuty finding for credential use from unexpected geography
- AWS CloudTrail showing API calls from a user-agent or source IP not in the expected baseline
- Sudden bill spike (mining instances)

Remediation runbook:
1. Deactivate the IAM key immediately, do not just rotate (rotation gives attacker time)
2. Audit CloudTrail for all actions taken with the key
3. Look for backdoors: new IAM users, roles, trust policies, lambda functions
4. Rotate any data or credentials reachable from the key's permissions
5. Cost-recover: AWS support will often credit fraud-related spend if remediated quickly

Anti-patterns:
- Force-pushing the offending commit and assuming the secret is gone — clones/forks/CI logs still have it
- Long-lived IAM access keys for CI when GitHub OIDC federation is available
- Storing secrets in CI environment variables instead of a real secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault)

metadata.title: AWS access key committed to public repo (or even private repo with broad access)

text:
Malicious npm/pip package included via dependency confusion or typosquat

Attacker publishes a package mimicking a legitimate one (typosquat) or exploits dependency confusion (publishing a public package with the same name as an internal one to a public registry; the build system pulls the public one). Build pipeline installs the malicious package; postinstall script exfiltrates env vars including AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and CI tokens.

Preventive controls:
- PIN dependencies with lockfiles AND verify integrity (npm `--ignore-scripts` for CI; pip-compile + hash mode)
- USE a private registry (Verdaccio, GitHub Packages, AWS CodeArtifact) configured to NEVER fall through to the public registry for internal scopes
- NAMESPACE internal packages with a scope (@company/foo) and reserve the scope on npmjs.com
- RUN dependency scanners (Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check, Dependabot) and BLOCK builds on critical findings
- DISABLE postinstall scripts in CI (npm ci `--ignore-scripts`) for any build that does not absolutely need them
- GENERATE and verify SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) on every build for downstream attestation

Detection signals:
- Sudden new package in lockfile diff — review every dependency add in code review
- Build CPU/network spike during install (postinstall scripts doing work)
- Egress traffic from CI runner to unknown domains during install
- GuardDuty findings on CI runner credentials used from anomalous IPs

Remediation runbook:
1. Remove the malicious package, lock to a known-good version
2. Rotate every credential the CI build had access to (AWS, registry, signing keys, deploy tokens)
3. Re-issue any artifacts the compromised build produced
4. Audit downstream consumers of those artifacts

Anti-patterns:
- Trusting `latest` tag for any dependency — pin versions
- Allowing public-registry fallthrough for internal scopes — opens dependency confusion door
- Running `npm install` in CI instead of `npm ci` — non-reproducible, ignores lockfile

metadata.title: Malicious npm/pip package included via dependency confusion or typosquat

text:
Bad deploy + missing PodDisruptionBudget + aggressive autoscaler = full outage

A new deploy ships a regression. HPA detects elevated error rate as elevated CPU and scales up. New pods are unhealthy. Cluster Autoscaler removes 'idle' nodes to save cost, evicting healthy pods at the same time the rolling deploy progresses. With no PodDisruptionBudget, kube-controller-manager evicts in parallel. All replicas of the service are unavailable simultaneously.

Preventive controls:
- DEFINE PodDisruptionBudget (`minAvailable: 1` or `maxUnavailable: 25%`) for every Deployment in production
- HEALTH PROBES: separate liveness, readiness, and startup probes — readiness gates traffic, liveness restarts, startup tolerates slow boots
- PROGRESSIVE delivery: Argo Rollouts or Flagger with metric-based analysis — auto-rollback on error rate / latency regression
- DEPLOY across multiple AZs with topology spread constraints — single-AZ failure does not kill the service
- PIN HPA min-replicas to ≥2 for any prod service — 'scale to zero' is for dev/staging

Detection signals:
- PodDisruptionBudget violation events in audit log
- Sudden drop in `kube_deployment_status_replicas_available`
- Error budget burn-rate alert (multi-window: fast burn 1h + slow burn 6h)
- Synthetic check failures coinciding with deploy timestamp

Remediation runbook:
1. Roll back the deploy via Argo Rollouts abort or `kubectl rollout undo`
2. Pause autoscaler until incident is closed
3. Add PDB before next deploy attempt
4. Postmortem — was the regression caught in staging? If not, why not?

Anti-patterns:
- No readiness probe — Kubernetes sends traffic to a pod that has not yet warmed up
- Liveness probe identical to readiness probe — restart loop on transient backend failure
- PDB `minAvailable: 100%` — blocks all evictions including legitimate node maintenance
- HPA scaling on CPU when error rate is the real signal

metadata.title: Bad deploy + missing PodDisruptionBudget + aggressive autoscaler = full outage

text:
Mandatory SecurityContext for all pods (CIS 5.2)

Every Pod must define a restrictive SecurityContext. Pod-level: runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1001, runAsGroup: 1001, fsGroup: 1001, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault. Container-level: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities.drop: [ALL]. Mount emptyDir for /tmp if read-only filesystem is set.

Decision rules:
- Apply both pod-level and container-level SecurityContext — they are complementary
- Use seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault to restrict system calls
- Mount emptyDir volumes at paths that require write access (e.g. /tmp)

Trade-offs:
- readOnlyRootFilesystem may break applications that write to the container filesystem — identify and mount emptyDir for those paths

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying pods without any SecurityContext
- Setting allowPrivilegeEscalation: true or omitting it (defaults to true without explicit false)

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- EKS enforces Pod Security Standards — set namespace labels pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted

metadata.title: Mandatory SecurityContext for all pods (CIS 5.2)

text:
RBAC with least privilege (CIS 5.1)

Create a dedicated ServiceAccount per application with automountServiceAccountToken: false. Define a Role with only required verbs on required resources. Bind via RoleBinding. Do not grant access to secrets unless strictly necessary.

Decision rules:
- Create a dedicated ServiceAccount for each workload — never use the default ServiceAccount
- Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on ServiceAccount to prevent token auto-mounting
- Grant only required verbs (get, list) on required resources — never use wildcard (*)

Trade-offs:
- Fine-grained RBAC requires understanding of which API resources each workload actually accesses

Anti-patterns:
- Using the default ServiceAccount for application workloads
- Granting cluster-admin or wildcard permissions to application ServiceAccounts
- Adding secrets to the Role resource list without justification

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Map to EKS IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) for AWS API access from pods

metadata.title: RBAC with least privilege (CIS 5.1)

text:
Network isolation with default-deny NetworkPolicy (CIS 5.3)

Apply a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy in each namespace (podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]). Then add explicit allow policies per service. Example: allow Ingress from ingress-nginx namespace on port 8000 only for pods matching app=api.

Decision rules:
- Start with a default-deny-all policy in every namespace
- Add explicit ingress and egress allow rules only for required traffic paths
- Use namespaceSelector for cross-namespace traffic (e.g. allowing ingress controller)

Trade-offs:
- NetworkPolicy requires a CNI plugin that supports it (Calico, Cilium, Weave) — does not work with Flannel alone

Anti-patterns:
- Operating namespaces with no NetworkPolicy (all traffic allowed by default)
- Using podSelector: {} in allow policies without scoping by policyTypes

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use VPC CNI with Calico on EKS for NetworkPolicy enforcement
- Complement with Security Groups for Pods on EKS for L4 controls

metadata.title: Network isolation with default-deny NetworkPolicy (CIS 5.3)

text:
Secrets management with External Secrets Operator (CIS 5.4)

Use External Secrets Operator (ESO) or Sealed Secrets instead of plain Kubernetes Secret manifests. ESO ExternalSecret references a SecretStore (e.g. vault-backend) and syncs secrets into a Kubernetes Secret. ConfigMaps should hold only non-sensitive configuration.

Decision rules:
- Never commit plain Kubernetes Secret manifests with base64-encoded values to version control
- Use External Secrets Operator to sync from AWS Secrets Manager, Vault, or GCP Secret Manager
- Use ConfigMaps exclusively for non-sensitive configuration (APP_ENV, LOG_LEVEL)

Trade-offs:
- ESO adds operational complexity — requires installing the controller and configuring SecretStore
- Sealed Secrets is simpler but less flexible — secrets can only be decrypted by the cluster

Anti-patterns:
- Storing database URLs or passwords in ConfigMaps (not encrypted at rest)
- Committing Kubernetes Secrets with real credentials to git repositories

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use ESO with AWS Secrets Manager provider on EKS
- Use Secrets Store CSI Driver with AWS SSM Parameter Store as an alternative

metadata.title: Secrets management with External Secrets Operator (CIS 5.4)

text:
Mandatory resource requests and limits (CIS 5.2.4)

Every container must define both resources.requests and resources.limits. Example: requests memory 128Mi cpu 100m, limits memory 512Mi cpu 500m. Without limits, a single pod can starve other workloads on the node.

Decision rules:
- Define both requests (scheduler hint) and limits (enforcement) for every container
- Use LimitRange objects to enforce defaults for namespaces missing explicit resource declarations

Trade-offs:
- Limits that are too tight cause OOMKilled events or CPU throttling — profile workloads before setting values

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying containers with no resource limits to shared cluster nodes
- Setting limits without requests — scheduler cannot make optimal placement decisions

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- EKS node autoscaling (Karpenter) uses requests to pack pods onto nodes efficiently

metadata.title: Mandatory resource requests and limits (CIS 5.2.4)

text:
Liveness and Readiness probes for workload health

Define livenessProbe (restarts unhealthy pods: httpGet /health, initialDelaySeconds 15, periodSeconds 20, failureThreshold 3) and readinessProbe (removes unhealthy pods from Service endpoints: httpGet /ready, initialDelaySeconds 5, periodSeconds 10) for every container.

Decision rules:
- Use readinessProbe to control traffic routing — pod is only added to Service endpoints when ready
- Use livenessProbe to restart pods stuck in an unrecoverable state
- Set startupProbe for slow-starting applications to prevent premature liveness failures

Trade-offs:
- Overly aggressive liveness probes (short timeouts, low failureThreshold) cause unnecessary restarts
- Missing readiness probes cause traffic to be sent to not-yet-ready pods

Anti-patterns:
- Using the same endpoint and thresholds for both liveness and readiness probes
- Not defining any health probes — Kubernetes cannot detect application-level failures

metadata.title: Liveness and Readiness probes for workload health

text:
Pod Disruption Budget for high availability

A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) limits voluntary disruptions (node drains, rolling updates). Example: minAvailable: 2 with selector app=api ensures at least 2 pods remain available during node maintenance.

Decision rules:
- Create a PDB for every production Deployment with more than 1 replica
- Use minAvailable (absolute) or maxUnavailable (percentage) depending on SLO requirements

Trade-offs:
- PDB with minAvailable equal to replicas will block node drains — leave at least 1 pod drainable

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying multi-replica workloads without a PDB — all pods may be disrupted simultaneously
- Setting minAvailable: 0 — defeats the purpose of the PDB

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- PDB works with EKS Managed Node Groups during node version upgrades

metadata.title: Pod Disruption Budget for high availability

text:
Ingress with TLS termination

Configure Ingress with TLS using cert-manager (cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod). Annotations: ssl-redirect: true, force-ssl-redirect: true. TLS spec references a Secret containing the certificate. All HTTP traffic redirected to HTTPS at the ingress level.

Decision rules:
- Always terminate TLS at the Ingress — never expose plain HTTP to the internet
- Use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt for automated certificate provisioning and renewal
- Set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: true to enforce HTTPS

Trade-offs:
- Let's Encrypt rate limits apply — use staging issuer for testing
- Certificate renewal requires outbound internet access from the cluster for ACME challenges

Anti-patterns:
- Exposing services over HTTP in production
- Using self-signed certificates without a trust chain (causes browser/client warnings)

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Alternatively use AWS ALB Ingress Controller with ACM certificates on EKS

metadata.title: Ingress with TLS termination

text:
Namespace and label conventions for production

Create a dedicated Namespace for each environment or team with labels: environment, managed-by, team. Standard labels applied to all resources: app (service name), version (semver), environment. Namespaces provide resource isolation, RBAC scope, and NetworkPolicy boundaries.

Decision rules:
- Use one namespace per environment (production, staging, development) — do not mix environments
- Apply consistent labels (app, version, environment) to all resources to enable selectors and monitoring
- Set managed-by: terraform or managed-by: helm on namespaces created via IaC

Trade-offs:
- Fine-grained namespace-per-team increases isolation but requires more RBAC and NetworkPolicy configuration

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying production workloads to the default namespace
- Omitting labels — makes resource selection, monitoring dashboards, and GitOps tooling fragile

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- EKS namespaces map to IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) scope for granular AWS API access control

metadata.title: Namespace and label conventions for production

text:
Production-ready Deployment manifest

Production Deployment: 3 replicas, RollingUpdate strategy (maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 for zero-downtime), dedicated ServiceAccount (automountServiceAccountToken: false), podAntiAffinity across nodes, pod-level SecurityContext (runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile RuntimeDefault), container-level SecurityContext (allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities drop ALL), resource requests/limits, env from ConfigMap/Secret, liveness + readiness + startup probes, emptyDir volumes for writable paths, terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60.

Decision rules:
- Set maxUnavailable: 0 for zero-downtime rolling deployments — pods are added before old ones are removed
- Use pinned image tags (myapp:1.0.0) — never :latest in production
- Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds >= timeout of your longest in-flight request to allow graceful shutdown

Trade-offs:
- maxUnavailable: 0 requires cluster capacity for maxSurge extra pods during rollout
- podAntiAffinity with preferredDuringScheduling may not spread pods if cluster nodes are insufficient

Anti-patterns:
- Using :latest image tag — non-deterministic and bypasses rollback capability
- Not setting terminationGracePeriodSeconds — pods may be killed mid-request
- Missing startup probe for slow-starting apps — liveness probe will kill the pod before it finishes initializing

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use Karpenter on EKS for just-in-time node provisioning to support rolling surge capacity

metadata.title: Production-ready Deployment manifest

text:
Service (ClusterIP) and Ingress with TLS

Service type ClusterIP on port 80 -> targetPort 8000. Never NodePort or LoadBalancer directly for internal services. Ingress with nginx ingress class, cert-manager annotation (letsencrypt-prod), ssl-redirect: true, proxy-body-size: 10m, rate-limit: 100. TLS spec with hosts array and secretName for certificate.

Decision rules:
- Use ClusterIP as the default Service type — expose externally only via Ingress
- Set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rate-limit on all public-facing Ingress resources
- Use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt for automated TLS certificate management

Trade-offs:
- Nginx Ingress with rate-limit annotation is per-server, not distributed — use Redis-backed rate limiting for distributed enforcement

Anti-patterns:
- Using NodePort or direct LoadBalancer Service types without an Ingress — bypasses centralized TLS and rate limiting
- Not setting proxy-body-size — allows unbounded request body sizes

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- On EKS, use AWS Load Balancer Controller with Ingress class alb for native ALB integration and ACM certificate management

metadata.title: Service (ClusterIP) and Ingress with TLS

text:
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) for automatic scaling

HPA (autoscaling/v2): scaleTargetRef points to the Deployment, minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 10. Metrics: CPU target utilization 70%, Memory target utilization 80%. Kubernetes scales pod count up/down to maintain the target metric values.

Decision rules:
- Set minReplicas >= 2 for production availability — 1 replica has no fault tolerance
- Use CPU utilization 70% as a target — leaves headroom before pods become saturated
- Combine HPA with PodDisruptionBudget to prevent all replicas from being disrupted simultaneously

Trade-offs:
- HPA reacts to current load — not suitable for sudden traffic spikes; use KEDA for event-driven scaling
- Memory-based scaling can cause scale-thrash if memory is not released promptly after load drops

Anti-patterns:
- Setting minReplicas: 1 in production — a single pod disruption causes a complete outage
- Setting maxReplicas too high without resource quotas — a runaway HPA can exhaust cluster capacity

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Combine HPA with Karpenter on EKS for both pod and node autoscaling
- Use KEDA with SQS queue depth metric for event-driven HPA on EKS

metadata.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) for automatic scaling

text:
ConfigMap and Secret configuration management

ConfigMap holds non-sensitive configuration: APP_ENV, LOG_LEVEL, CORS_ORIGINS, MAX_CONNECTIONS. Secrets hold sensitive values (DATABASE_URL) but in production should be managed via External Secrets Operator, not committed as plain Secret manifests. Reference ConfigMap values with valueFrom.configMapKeyRef, Secrets with valueFrom.secretKeyRef.

Decision rules:
- ConfigMap is for non-sensitive configuration only — never put passwords or tokens in ConfigMap
- In production: use External Secrets Operator to sync from AWS Secrets Manager into Kubernetes Secrets
- Reference individual keys (configMapKeyRef, secretKeyRef) rather than envFrom for explicit env var declarations

Trade-offs:
- envFrom (whole ConfigMap/Secret as env vars) is simpler but makes pod environment unpredictable — prefer key-by-key references

Anti-patterns:
- Storing sensitive values in ConfigMap data (not encrypted at rest by default)
- Committing Secret manifests with base64-encoded values to git — base64 is encoding, not encryption

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Use External Secrets Operator with AWS Secrets Manager SecretStore for EKS
- Use Secrets Store CSI Driver with AWS SSM Parameter Store as an alternative

metadata.title: ConfigMap and Secret configuration management

text:
Minimal Kubernetes Deployment and ClusterIP Service

Minimal Kubernetes Deployment and Service manifests for a backend container. Deployment (apps/v1): 1 replica, selector app=backend, container image backend:latest on containerPort 8080. Service (v1): ClusterIP type, selector app=backend, port 8080 -> targetPort 8080.

Decision rules:
- Use as a baseline template for any backend service Kubernetes deployment
- Service type ClusterIP — accessible only within the cluster; add Ingress for external access

Trade-offs:
- Single replica with no HPA — not suitable for production traffic without scaling configuration
- No resource requests/limits — must be added to prevent resource starvation
- No SecurityContext — extend with runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities drop ALL per CIS Kubernetes Benchmark

Anti-patterns:
- Do not use image:latest in production — pin to a specific tag or image digest
- Do not deploy without resource limits to shared cluster namespaces

metadata.title: Minimal Kubernetes Deployment and ClusterIP Service

text:
Pods — The Atomic Scheduling Unit

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — a logical host for one or more tightly coupled containers sharing a network namespace and storage volumes. Pods are ephemeral by design: they can be killed, rescheduled, and replaced at any time. The AI agent must understand that pods are NEVER managed directly in production; they are always controlled by a higher-level workload controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, Job). The Pod spec defines resource requests, limits, probes, security context, and volume mounts — all of which are critical to scheduling decisions and production stability.

Decision rules:
- NEVER create raw Pods directly in production — always use a controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, Job, DaemonSet)
- USE a single-container Pod as the default pattern — multi-container pods (sidecars) only for logging agents, service mesh proxies, or config synchronizers tightly coupled to the main app
- ASSUME every Pod will be rescheduled — design applications to be stateless and re-entrant by default
- SIZE Pod resource requests based on the p95 observed CPU/memory from load tests — not guesses
- USE init containers for database migration or dependency readiness checks — run sequentially before the main container starts
- APPLY pod anti-affinity rules for critical workloads to prevent multiple replicas from landing on the same node — single node failure must not cause full outage

Trade-offs:
- Single-container pods: simplicity and debuggability vs. cannot share in-process communication with sidecars
- Multi-container pods (sidecars): powerful for service mesh, logging, auth proxy vs. increases scheduling complexity and restarts one container may kill healthy siblings
- Ephemeral pods: horizontal scalability vs. any in-memory state is lost on reschedule — forces good application design
- Init containers: clean dependency ordering vs. add startup latency — bad choice for very fast-starting apps

Anti-patterns:
- Running pods with no resource requests — Kubernetes scheduler cannot make correct node placement decisions, leads to noisy-neighbor OOM kills
- Using Pod hostNetwork: true in production — bypasses Kubernetes network isolation and makes port conflicts likely
- Storing persistent data in Pod ephemeral storage (emptyDir) and expecting it to survive restarts
- Running multiple unrelated services in a single Pod — violates single-responsibility, breaks independent scaling
- Pinning Pods to specific nodes with nodeName — bypasses scheduler, breaks cluster autoscaling

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: pod anti-affinity across AZs mirrors the multi-AZ redundancy principle of AWS Well-Architected
- Security Pillar: pod-level security context (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem) aligns with least-privilege compute
- Performance Efficiency: right-sized resource requests enable bin-packing and Karpenter node provisioning accuracy

metadata.title: Pods — The Atomic Scheduling Unit

text:
Deployments — Stateless Workload Controller

A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which in turn manages identical Pod replicas. It is the primary controller for stateless applications. Deployments provide declarative rollout strategies, rollback capability, and replica scaling. The Deployment's spec.strategy field controls how updates are rolled out — the choice of strategy (RollingUpdate vs Recreate) has direct production availability implications. In EKS, Deployments are the default workload type for APIs, web services, background processors, and any application where all replicas are identical.

Decision rules:
- USE Deployments for ALL stateless workloads — APIs, frontends, background workers consuming from queues
- USE RollingUpdate strategy (default) for zero-downtime updates — set maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1 for production-critical services
- USE Recreate strategy ONLY when the application cannot run two versions simultaneously (e.g., database schema lock) and a brief downtime is acceptable
- SET minReadySeconds to ensure pods are truly healthy before being counted as available — prevents premature rollout completion
- USE Deployment revisionHistoryLimit: 5 in production — enables kubectl rollout undo to any of the last 5 revisions
- SCALE Deployments horizontally (increase replicas) before scaling vertically (increase resource limits) — horizontal scaling is cheaper and faster in EKS

Trade-offs:
- RollingUpdate: zero downtime vs. two versions running simultaneously requires backward-compatible APIs
- Recreate: simple version transition vs. guaranteed downtime window during updates
- High replica count: fault tolerance and throughput vs. higher baseline cost and more complex scheduling
- Deployment vs. StatefulSet: Deployments are simpler but assume replicas are interchangeable — breaks for stateful apps

Anti-patterns:
- Using StatefulSets for stateless applications — wastes ordered pod management overhead with no benefit
- Setting maxUnavailable: 50% on single-digit replica counts — kills too many pods at once, causes partial outages
- Not setting resource limits on Deployment pods — one misbehaving deployment can starve the entire node
- Deploying with spec.replicas: 1 in production — single point of failure, no rolling update capability
- Using image tag 'latest' in Deployment spec — prevents rollback, causes non-deterministic behavior

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0 is the EKS-recommended pattern for zero-downtime deploys
- Operational Excellence: revision history enables rapid rollback — supports mean-time-to-recovery (MTTR) targets
- EKS Best Practices: Deployments work natively with ALB Ingress Controller and HPA for auto-scaling

metadata.title: Deployments — Stateless Workload Controller

text:
Services — Internal Networking (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer)

A Kubernetes Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name for a dynamic set of Pods selected by label. Services decouple consumers from the Pod lifecycle — Pods are replaced, the Service endpoint persists. There are three primary types relevant to production EKS: ClusterIP (internal only), NodePort (node-level port exposure), and LoadBalancer (provisions an AWS load balancer). On EKS, the LoadBalancer type is managed by the AWS Load Balancer Controller and provisions either ALB or NLB resources. ClusterIP is the correct default; LoadBalancer should be used sparingly.

Decision rules:
- USE ClusterIP as the default Service type for all internal microservice-to-microservice communication
- USE LoadBalancer type ONLY when the service must be directly internet-facing and an Ingress is not appropriate (e.g., TCP-level services, gRPC without HTTP/2 termination at the ALB)
- USE NodePort ONLY for local development or legacy on-premises load balancer integration — never in standard EKS production
- PREFER Ingress + ClusterIP over creating one LoadBalancer Service per application — multiple LoadBalancer services multiply NLB/ALB costs
- USE Service type ExternalName to create CNAME aliases to external services (RDS endpoint, ElastiCache) — keeps DNS resolution internal to cluster
- SET sessionAffinity: ClientIP for Services fronting stateful in-memory sessions that cannot be migrated — understand this breaks horizontal scaling

Trade-offs:
- ClusterIP: zero external cost, fully isolated vs. requires Ingress or VPN to expose externally
- LoadBalancer per service: direct L4 access, simple vs. one ALB/NLB per service = high cost at scale
- Shared Ingress + ClusterIP: cost-efficient, feature-rich routing vs. adds Ingress controller as a shared dependency
- NodePort: works without cloud integration vs. exposes arbitrary high ports, requires security group management

Anti-patterns:
- Creating a LoadBalancer Service for every microservice — at 20 services, this means 20 ALBs ($20+/month each minimum)
- Using NodePort in production without a managed load balancer in front — exposes node IPs directly
- Not setting Service port names — breaks Istio/Envoy protocol detection and metrics labeling
- Omitting selector on a Service without intentionally creating a headless service — results in a Service with no endpoints

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: shared ALB via Ingress reduces per-service load balancer costs by 60-80%
- Security Pillar: ClusterIP services are not reachable from outside the VPC — reduces attack surface
- EKS Best Practices: AWS Load Balancer Controller is the recommended way to manage AWS ELB resources from Kubernetes

metadata.title: Services — Internal Networking (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer)

text:
Ingress — L7 Routing, TLS Termination, and Path-Based Rules

Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that manages external HTTP/HTTPS access to Services inside the cluster. It provides L7 features: host-based routing, path-based routing, TLS termination, and header manipulation. On EKS, an Ingress is reconciled by the AWS Load Balancer Controller into an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Multiple Ingress resources can share a single ALB using IngressGroup annotations — a critical cost optimization. Ingress is the canonical entry point for HTTP workloads on EKS; using a raw LoadBalancer Service for HTTP traffic is an anti-pattern.

Decision rules:
- USE Ingress for ALL HTTP/HTTPS workloads — it maps to ALB which provides SSL termination, WAF integration, and path routing
- USE alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name annotation to share one ALB across multiple Ingress resources — reduces ALB cost from O(n) to O(1)
- USE IngressClass to select between ALB (HTTP) and NLB (TCP) — choose based on protocol requirements, not preference
- TERMINATE TLS at the ALB using ACM certificates — never serve plain HTTP in production, never manage TLS certs inside pods
- USE host-based routing for multi-tenant or multi-service cluster — api.example.com and app.example.com on one ALB
- USE path-based routing (/api/*, /web/*) for monolith decomposition — enables gradual service extraction without DNS changes

Trade-offs:
- ALB Ingress: rich L7 features, WAF, native AWS integration vs. ALB provisioning takes 1-3 minutes on first apply
- Nginx Ingress Controller: battle-tested, rich annotation set vs. requires managing the controller itself as a Deployment
- Shared ALB (IngressGroup): cost-efficient vs. one misconfigured Ingress can affect all services sharing the ALB
- TLS at ALB: simpler pod config vs. traffic inside VPC is unencrypted (mitigated by VPC isolation)

Anti-patterns:
- Not using IngressGroup — results in one ALB per Ingress, 10 services = 10 ALBs = 10x ALB cost
- Handling TLS termination inside pods — complex certificate rotation, no WAF capability, no access logs in ALB
- Using wildcard path /* with a single backend — defeats the purpose of Ingress routing, better to use a LoadBalancer Service
- Deploying Ingress without readiness probe on backend pods — ALB registers unhealthy targets, returns 502 errors

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: ALB + ACM + WAF integration satisfies encryption-in-transit and perimeter defense requirements
- Cost Optimization: IngressGroup sharing one ALB across a service mesh is the AWS-recommended pattern
- EKS Blueprints: AWS Load Balancer Controller is a required add-on in all EKS Blueprint reference architectures

metadata.title: Ingress — L7 Routing, TLS Termination, and Path-Based Rules

text:
ConfigMaps & Secrets — Configuration Separation Strategy

ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs. Secrets store sensitive data (passwords, tokens, certificates) in base64-encoded form. On EKS, the production pattern is NOT to use native Kubernetes Secrets for sensitive values — because they are stored in etcd base64-encoded (not encrypted at rest unless envelope encryption is configured). The AWS-native production pattern is: store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, and use the External Secrets Operator or Secrets Store CSI Driver to sync them into pods. ConfigMaps are safe for non-sensitive config and are the correct tool for application configuration injection.

Decision rules:
- USE ConfigMaps for non-sensitive configuration: feature flags, log levels, external API endpoints, connection pool sizes
- NEVER store real credentials, API keys, or passwords in ConfigMaps — even base64 values — use Secrets or better
- USE AWS Secrets Manager + External Secrets Operator (ESO) for all sensitive values in production EKS — ESO syncs ASM secrets as Kubernetes Secrets automatically
- USE Secrets Store CSI Driver when you need secrets mounted as files (TLS certs, SSH keys) without creating Kubernetes Secret objects
- ENABLE EKS envelope encryption (KMS CMK) for etcd Secrets if you must use native Kubernetes Secrets — required for compliance (PCI, HIPAA)
- MOUNT ConfigMaps as environment variables for simple key-value config; mount as volume files for multi-line config (nginx.conf, application.yaml)

Trade-offs:
- Native Kubernetes Secrets: simple, no external dependency vs. not truly encrypted without KMS envelope encryption
- External Secrets Operator: production-grade, centralized secret management vs. additional controller to manage, adds AWS API dependency
- Secrets Store CSI Driver: secrets as files, no etcd persistence vs. more complex pod spec, SPIFFE/SVID integration needed for zero-trust
- ConfigMap volume mount: supports config reload without pod restart (via inotify) vs. more complex than env vars, requires app to watch for changes

Anti-patterns:
- Committing Kubernetes Secret YAML with base64 values to Git — base64 is encoding, not encryption; anyone with repo access has the secret
- Creating one ConfigMap for an entire cluster namespace — changes to any key trigger unnecessary pod restarts for unrelated services
- Using Secrets for non-sensitive configuration — not an error but adds unnecessary RBAC complexity
- Not rotating secrets — External Secrets Operator supports automatic rotation; not using it means manual credential rotation
- Storing secrets in container image layers (ENV Dockerfile instructions) — baked into image, not rotatable

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: AWS Secrets Manager + ESO is the EKS Best Practices recommended pattern for secret management
- Operational Excellence: ESO automatic rotation reduces manual secret rotation toil
- Reliability Pillar: KMS envelope encryption for etcd satisfies AWS compliance requirements for regulated industries

metadata.title: ConfigMaps & Secrets — Configuration Separation Strategy

text:
Persistent Volumes — Stateful Storage Decisions on EKS

Persistent Volumes (PVs) and Persistent Volume Claims (PVCs) decouple storage from Pod lifecycle. On EKS, PVs are dynamically provisioned by the EBS CSI Driver (block storage) or EFS CSI Driver (shared file system). The storage class chosen determines the AWS storage backing. The critical architectural decision is whether to use in-cluster persistent storage at all — AWS-managed database services (RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB) are almost always preferable to running stateful databases inside EKS. In-cluster PVs are appropriate for specific use cases: CI/CD runners, ML training data staging, message brokers, search engines.

Decision rules:
- PREFER AWS managed services (RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB, OpenSearch) over running databases inside EKS — reduces operational complexity, provides automatic backups, Multi-AZ, and managed failover
- USE EBS-backed PVs (gp3 storage class) for stateful workloads that require block storage and run as a single replica: Elasticsearch, Kafka, single-instance databases
- USE EFS-backed PVs for ReadWriteMany (RWX) use cases: shared ML training datasets, CMS media uploads, CI/CD workspace sharing across pods
- USE StatefulSets with volumeClaimTemplates for stateful workloads in Kubernetes — each pod gets its own PVC, guarantees stable pod identity
- SET storage class reclaim policy to Retain (not Delete) for production PVs — prevents accidental data loss when PVC is deleted
- SIZE PVs with 20-30% headroom above current usage — EBS volumes cannot be dynamically shrunk, only expanded

Trade-offs:
- EBS PV: high IOPS, low latency vs. zone-locked (a PV in us-east-1a cannot attach to a pod in us-east-1b), breaks multi-AZ scheduling
- EFS PV: ReadWriteMany, multi-AZ vs. higher latency than EBS (10-20ms vs <1ms), significantly higher cost per GB
- In-cluster database: full control, cost potentially lower vs. you own all operational concerns: backup, failover, upgrades, scaling
- Managed RDS vs. in-cluster PostgreSQL: full-managed, HA, automatic failover vs. managed Postgres can cost 3-5x more for identical specs

Anti-patterns:
- Running production databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) inside Kubernetes without a deep Kubernetes-native operator like CloudNativePG or Vitess — bare Deployments with PVCs break on node failure
- Using EBS PVs with Deployments (not StatefulSets) with replicas > 1 — EBS is ReadWriteOnce, multiple pods cannot mount the same volume
- Not configuring a VolumeSnapshot schedule for production PVs — EBS snapshots are not automatic, data loss risk on pod/node failure
- Using hostPath volumes in production — data tied to a specific node, breaks scheduler freedom, security risk

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: AWS managed databases provide Multi-AZ failover that is extremely difficult to replicate with in-cluster stateful sets
- Operational Excellence: EBS CSI Driver is a required EKS managed add-on — use it instead of the deprecated in-tree AWS storage driver
- Cost Optimization: gp3 EBS is 20% cheaper than gp2 with better baseline performance — always default to gp3 storage class

metadata.title: Persistent Volumes — Stateful Storage Decisions on EKS

text:
Stateless Applications — The Ideal Kubernetes Workload

Stateless applications are the canonical Kubernetes workload. A stateless application stores no client-specific data locally between requests — all state lives in external systems (database, cache, object storage). Stateless pods are interchangeable, can be killed and rescheduled without data loss, and can be scaled horizontally without coordination. Kubernetes is specifically designed to excel at managing stateless workloads. Web APIs, REST services, GraphQL endpoints, frontend BFFs, and event-driven processors consuming from queues are all stateless patterns that map perfectly to Kubernetes Deployments.

Decision rules:
- CHOOSE Kubernetes for stateless workloads when: multiple replicas are needed, traffic is variable, or there are multiple services with different scaling needs
- USE Deployments with HPA for stateless workloads — pods are interchangeable, rolling updates are safe, horizontal scaling is linear
- ENSURE stateless applications externalize ALL state: use RDS/Aurora for persistent data, ElastiCache for session/cache, S3 for file storage
- CONFIGURE graceful shutdown (SIGTERM handler, terminationGracePeriodSeconds) — pods are terminated routinely and must drain in-flight requests cleanly
- DESIGN for fail-fast startup — stateless pods should be ready in < 30 seconds to enable rapid scale-out during traffic spikes
- WHEN traffic is very low (<100 req/day) and cost is the primary concern, PREFER Lambda over EKS for stateless HTTP handlers

Trade-offs:
- Stateless on EKS: horizontal scalability, resource efficiency vs. requires externalizing all state — adds dependency on RDS/ElastiCache
- Pod count vs. pod size: many small pods (better bin-packing, granular scaling) vs. fewer large pods (simpler operations, less scheduling overhead)
- EKS vs. Lambda for stateless: EKS has no cold start, persistent connections vs. Lambda auto-scales to zero, lower cost for spiky/low traffic

Anti-patterns:
- Storing user session data in pod memory — session lost on pod restart, breaks horizontal scaling (sticky sessions are a workaround, not a solution)
- Using pod-local file system as a temporary data store across requests — use S3 or EFS instead
- Running a stateless application with replicas: 1 — wastes the core value of Kubernetes, single point of failure
- Using EKS for a simple stateless function that runs < 5 minutes on a fixed schedule — CloudWatch Events + Lambda is dramatically simpler

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Performance Efficiency: stateless applications enable horizontal scaling — the Well-Architected pattern for scalable compute
- Reliability Pillar: no local state means pod failure has zero data impact — Kubernetes replaces the pod, service continues
- EKS Best Practices: EKS is designed as a stateless compute platform — stateful concerns are delegated to AWS managed services

metadata.title: Stateless Applications — The Ideal Kubernetes Workload

text:
Stateful Applications — StatefulSets, Operators, and the Managed Services Decision

Stateful applications maintain data between requests — databases, message brokers, search indices, ML model servers with local weights. Kubernetes can run stateful workloads via StatefulSets, which provide: stable network identities (pod-0, pod-1), stable storage (PVC per pod), and ordered deployment/scaling. However, running production databases inside Kubernetes requires a Kubernetes-native operator (CloudNativePG, Strimzi for Kafka, Redis Operator) that understands the application's failover semantics. The AI agent must evaluate: is the complexity of running this stateful workload on Kubernetes justified, or should it use an AWS managed service?

Decision rules:
- DEFAULT to AWS managed services for stateful data: RDS/Aurora for SQL, ElastiCache for Redis/Memcached, MSK for Kafka, OpenSearch for Elasticsearch
- USE StatefulSet + Kubernetes Operator for stateful workloads ONLY when: the AWS managed service is cost-prohibitive at scale, you need specific database extensions not supported by RDS, or multi-cloud portability is a hard requirement
- NEVER run stateful workloads in Kubernetes without a production-grade operator — bare StatefulSets for databases have no automated failover
- USE StatefulSets (not Deployments) for all workloads requiring stable network identity: Kafka, ZooKeeper, Cassandra, Elasticsearch
- PLAN for PodDisruptionBudgets on StatefulSets — ensure quorum is maintained during node drain, cluster upgrades, and Spot interruptions
- WHEN running Kafka on EKS: prefer Amazon MSK for managed Kafka, reserve self-managed Strimzi only when MSK limits are hit (custom broker configs, extreme throughput)

Trade-offs:
- Managed RDS: fully managed HA, automated backups, Multi-AZ vs. 2-5x more expensive than equivalent self-managed PostgreSQL on EC2/EKS
- Stateful on EKS: cost control, full configuration access vs. you own: backups, failover, upgrades, replication, DR
- Kubernetes Operators: automate complex stateful operations vs. operator bugs can cause split-brain or data loss — maturity matters
- MSK vs. Kafka on EKS: AWS manages brokers, ZooKeeper, TLS vs. lose ability to tune broker JVM, custom MirrorMaker configs

Anti-patterns:
- Running MySQL/PostgreSQL in a bare Kubernetes Deployment with a PVC and single replica — this is a data loss time-bomb, not a production database
- Using Recreate strategy for StatefulSet updates — causes complete database downtime, never appropriate for HA databases
- Not setting up PodDisruptionBudgets for quorum-based systems (Kafka, Cassandra, ZooKeeper) — Kubernetes node drain can take down majority and cause leader election failure
- Mixing stateful and stateless workloads on the same node group — stateful pods with large PVCs cause node-level resource fragmentation

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: AWS managed services (RDS Multi-AZ, MSK) provide automated failover that self-managed stateful workloads cannot easily match
- Operational Excellence: choosing managed services reduces operational overhead — reserve StatefulSet complexity for cases where it pays off
- Cost Optimization: detailed TCO analysis required — managed service premium is often justified by reduced engineering hours on DB operations

metadata.title: Stateful Applications — StatefulSets, Operators, and the Managed Services Decision

text:
REST APIs and GraphQL Services — Scaling Patterns on EKS

REST APIs and GraphQL endpoints are the most common EKS workload type. They are inherently stateless, horizontally scalable, and have well-understood traffic patterns. EKS is an excellent platform for API workloads when: the API has consistent traffic, needs multiple microservices, or requires fine-grained scaling control. The key architectural decisions are: Ingress configuration, HPA metrics selection (CPU, custom metrics from Prometheus), connection pooling to backing databases, and circuit breaker patterns for inter-service calls.

Decision rules:
- USE EKS for API workloads when: > 3 independent services, sustained traffic (> 100 req/min baseline), team manages the container platform centrally
- USE Lambda for API workloads when: traffic is highly spiky or near-zero at rest, API response latency tolerance > 1 second, request duration < 15 minutes
- USE ECS Fargate for API workloads when: team wants managed containers without Kubernetes operational overhead, and microservices complexity is moderate (< 10 services)
- CONFIGURE HPA on CPU (70% target) as the baseline autoscaling metric for API pods — add custom metrics (requests-per-second from ALB via KEDA) for more accurate scaling
- IMPLEMENT connection pooling (PgBouncer for PostgreSQL, connection pool in app code) — pod count × max_connections must not exceed database max_connections limit
- SET up pod disruption budgets to maintain minimum available replicas during rolling updates — prevents momentary API unavailability during deploy

Trade-offs:
- EKS vs. Lambda for APIs: EKS has no cold start, persistent DB connections vs. Lambda scales to zero, lower cost at low traffic
- HPA CPU-based scaling: simple, zero-dependency vs. CPU is a lagging indicator — traffic spike may kill existing pods before new ones are ready
- HPA RPS-based scaling (KEDA): scales ahead of traffic vs. requires KEDA operator, Prometheus metrics pipeline, more complex setup
- Microservices API on EKS: independent deployability, scaling, fault isolation vs. distributed tracing required, inter-service latency adds up

Anti-patterns:
- Running a high-traffic API (> 10k RPS) on Lambda — cold starts, concurrency limits, and 15-minute timeout constraints make ECS/EKS a better fit
- Not implementing circuit breakers between microservices — one slow downstream service causes cascading failures across all API callers
- Exposing internal service-to-service APIs via LoadBalancer Service (external IP) — adds latency, cost, and attack surface; use ClusterIP + gRPC/HTTP2 internally
- Deploying all API services in the same namespace with no network policies — any compromised pod can reach all other services

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Performance Efficiency: HPA with ALB request metrics (via KEDA) enables proactive scaling before pod CPU climbs
- Reliability Pillar: PodDisruptionBudgets and minReadySeconds ensure rolling updates maintain minimum API availability
- Security Pillar: ALB WAF + network policies create defense-in-depth for public-facing API workloads

metadata.title: REST APIs and GraphQL Services — Scaling Patterns on EKS

text:
Background Workers — Queue Consumers and Async Processors

Background workers process messages from queues (SQS, Kafka, RabbitMQ) or events asynchronously. They are stateless, long-running, and often CPU/memory intensive. On EKS, background workers run as Deployments and scale based on queue depth rather than CPU. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) is the standard EKS add-on for scaling workers based on SQS queue depth, Kafka consumer group lag, or Redis list length. Background workers are an ideal EKS workload because they can scale from 0 to many replicas without affecting a user-facing SLA.

Decision rules:
- USE Deployments for background workers — they are stateless consumers; each pod processes independent messages
- USE KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaler) to scale worker replicas based on queue depth — SQS queue length, Kafka lag, or Redis list length are the correct scaling signals
- CONFIGURE KEDA minReplicaCount: 0 for cost-critical background workers — pods scale to zero when queue is empty, scale up when messages arrive
- PREFER EKS for background workers when: the worker is CPU/memory-intensive (video encoding, ML inference, PDF processing), runs for > 15 minutes, or needs GPU access
- PREFER Lambda for background workers when: processing time < 15 minutes, event volume is very spiky, and compute intensity is low
- SET appropriate SQS visibility timeout = 2x maximum processing time — prevents message reprocessing when a pod is slow but not failed

Trade-offs:
- KEDA scale-to-zero: eliminates idle worker cost vs. cold start latency when queue fills after idle period (pod startup time 30-90s)
- EKS workers vs. Lambda consumers: EKS can run for hours, uses any language/runtime vs. Lambda 15-minute limit, cold start on burst
- Single worker deployment vs. multiple specialized workers: simpler operations vs. different message types may need different resource profiles

Anti-patterns:
- Scaling background workers on CPU — CPU doesn't reflect queue backlog, pods idle with high queue depth while CPU is low
- Not implementing dead-letter queues (SQS DLQ) — poison messages that crash workers will loop indefinitely
- Running background workers without resource limits — a processing bug (infinite loop, memory leak) can OOM-kill the node
- Sharing the same node group with latency-sensitive API pods — bursty worker CPU usage causes noisy-neighbor latency spikes on API pods

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: KEDA scale-to-zero for SQS consumers eliminates idle compute cost — core Well-Architected cost optimization pattern
- Reliability Pillar: SQS DLQ + KEDA retry logic ensures no message loss on worker pod failure
- EKS Best Practices: KEDA is an EKS-supported add-on (available via EKS add-on marketplace) for event-driven scaling

metadata.title: Background Workers — Queue Consumers and Async Processors

text:
Batch Jobs — CronJobs, One-Shot Jobs, and Long-Running Compute

Batch workloads run to completion rather than serving ongoing traffic. Kubernetes provides two primitives: Job (run-once) and CronJob (scheduled, recurring). Jobs are appropriate for database migrations, report generation, data transformation pipelines, and ML training runs. CronJobs are appropriate for nightly ETL, scheduled reports, cache warming, and cleanup tasks. For large-scale parallel batch processing (Spark, Argo Workflows, data processing pipelines), EKS is the primary platform. For simple, infrequent batch tasks, AWS Batch (managed) or Lambda (short-duration) may be simpler.

Decision rules:
- USE Kubernetes Job for batch tasks that: run for > 15 minutes, need GPU, require specific container images/environments, or are part of a complex DAG (Argo Workflows)
- USE CronJob for scheduled recurring tasks — set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid to prevent overlapping runs when previous job is still running
- USE AWS Batch instead of Kubernetes Jobs when: the batch system team wants managed job scheduling without Kubernetes operational overhead, and jobs are independent (no DAG dependencies)
- USE Lambda for batch tasks when: duration < 15 minutes, triggered by S3 events or EventBridge schedules, and compute is lightweight
- SET activeDeadlineSeconds on all Jobs — prevents zombie jobs from running indefinitely and consuming cluster resources
- USE ttlSecondsAfterFinished on Jobs to auto-clean completed pods — prevents completed job pod accumulation cluttering the cluster

Trade-offs:
- Kubernetes Jobs vs. AWS Batch: full Kubernetes ecosystem integration vs. AWS Batch is managed, no node/scheduler management
- CronJob vs. EventBridge + Lambda: CronJob runs inside EKS (direct cluster access, shared VPC) vs. Lambda is serverless, no idle cost, but 15-minute limit
- Argo Workflows: powerful DAG orchestration, Kubernetes-native vs. significant complexity, requires dedicated operator and UI
- Spot instances for batch Jobs: 70% cost reduction vs. Spot interruption requires job checkpointing or idempotent retry design

Anti-patterns:
- Running batch Jobs on On-Demand nodes when jobs are interruptible — Spot instances are ideal for batch compute (Spot interruption gives 2-minute warning)
- CronJob without resource limits — scheduled jobs running at midnight can starve Spot nodes and impact daytime workloads
- Not setting backoffLimit on Jobs — failed jobs retry indefinitely, burning cluster resources and flooding logs
- Using Deployment instead of Job for finite-work tasks — Deployments restart completed containers, creating infinite retry loops

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: Spot node groups dedicated to batch workloads reduce batch compute cost by 60-70% vs. On-Demand
- Operational Excellence: ttlSecondsAfterFinished prevents cluster state accumulation — keeps control plane responsive
- EKS Best Practices: separate batch node groups from application node groups via node labels/taints — prevents batch-app resource contention

metadata.title: Batch Jobs — CronJobs, One-Shot Jobs, and Long-Running Compute

text:
Rolling Updates — Zero-Downtime Default Strategy

Rolling update is Kubernetes' default Deployment strategy. It incrementally replaces old Pods with new ones, ensuring a configurable number of healthy replicas are always running. It is the correct strategy for the vast majority of web services, APIs, and background workers. The critical parameters — maxUnavailable and maxSurge — directly control the trade-off between update speed and availability. In EKS, rolling updates integrate with the ALB's target group health checks — the ALB only routes traffic to ready pods, making zero-downtime deploys achievable without additional orchestration.

Decision rules:
- USE RollingUpdate as the default deployment strategy for all stateless HTTP services — it requires no additional infrastructure
- SET maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 for production API workloads — guarantees zero downtime, slightly slower rollout
- SET maxUnavailable: 25%, maxSurge: 25% for background workers where brief capacity reduction is acceptable — faster rollout
- COMBINE rolling update with readinessProbe — new pods only receive traffic after passing readiness checks, protecting users from partially-started instances
